Flow-Based Generative Models: When Probability Flows Like a Fluid

How the 18th-century mathematics of Euler made generative models faster to sample and simpler to train.

A reference such as P2:§3.8 points to Section 3.8 of post 2.

This is post #4 in the series Continuous-Time Generative Models. It builds directly on post #3, which derived the probability-flow ODE, the deterministic counterpart of the reverse-time SDE.

Diffusion models generate data by reversing a gradual transformation from data to noise. They learn the score of the intermediate distributions and use it to construct either a reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) or a deterministic probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE). The score determines the drift of the reverse-time SDE and, together with the forward dynamics, the velocity field of the probability-flow ODE. The SDE combines this drift with stochastic noise, whereas the ODE generates samples using only its deterministic velocity field. This raises a natural question: if generation with the probability-flow ODE requires only a velocity field, can we learn that field directly, by regression, without learning the score first?

Direct velocity learning is only part of the challenge. Diffusion models can require hundreds or thousands of network evaluations to generate a sample, their trajectories can curve and change speed, and the forward SDE fixes the path of distributions between data and noise. Generation also typically starts from Gaussian noise. We therefore want not just a way to learn velocity directly, but a simple and efficient way to learn a field whose trajectories are easy to solve.

We begin with normalizing flows, which transform a simple distribution into a data distribution through a sequence of invertible maps and provide exact likelihoods [1], [2]. Each map requires a tractable Jacobian determinant, restricting the choice of transformations and often requiring deep stacks to achieve sufficient expressiveness. Normalizing flows establish the idea of transporting probability distributions, but their discrete transformations can make the model cumbersome.

Flow models replace those transformations with an ODE [3]. Drawing their mathematics from Euler’s description of fluid motion [4], they represent generation through a time-dependent velocity field that transports noise toward data. Solving the ODE numerically generates samples, while the instantaneous change-of-variables formula gives their likelihoods. This replaces a stack of maps with continuous dynamics, but maximum-likelihood training still requires solving the ODE at each training step. Methods such as FFJORD [5] and RNODE [6] reduce this computational burden without eliminating it. Moreover, likelihood training does not prescribe the path between noise and data, leaving the model to discover suitable dynamics while optimizing its objective.

Flow matching takes the next step: instead of learning the velocity indirectly through likelihood optimization, it specifies a path of intermediate distributions and learns the velocity field by regression [7], [8], [9]. Training no longer requires solving the ODE. This also offers a different way to view the probability-flow ODE from post #3: rather than deriving its velocity from a learned score, we can train a velocity field directly.

The continuity equation, which expresses conservation of probability, describes how this field transports distributions along the chosen path. The post re-derives post #3’s probability-flow ODE from this equation. Unlike diffusion, flow matching allows us to choose the path rather than inherit it from a prescribed forward SDE.

But specifying the path of distributions does not tell us how individual samples should move along it. The continuity equation constrains the velocity field to transport the distributions correctly, but does not uniquely determine it. The marginal velocity field we want to learn, the particular one that flow matching regresses onto, is intractable, because it depends on the intractable density of the path, leaving us without a direct regression target.

Lipman et al. resolve this by constructing the desired path from simpler conditional paths, one for each data point, whose velocity fields are known analytically. Each conditional path describes how noise moves toward a particular data point. The continuity equation shows that averaging these conditional velocity fields, weighted by the posterior probability of each data point given the current sample, produces a velocity field that transports the marginal distributions along the desired path.

This gives us a tractable regression target, but one question remains: does learning the conditional velocity fields learn the desired marginal velocity field? Lipman et al. prove that the conditional and marginal regression objectives have the same gradient and differ only by a constant. Minimizing the conditional objective therefore learns the desired marginal dynamics without ever requiring the unknown marginal velocity field itself.

To make these conditional paths easy to construct, Lipman et al. choose paths that are Gaussian at each time given the data point. This choice also connects flow matching back to diffusion: the perturbation kernels of the Variance-Preserving (VP) and Variance-Exploding (VE) SDEs, with time reversed, are examples of such Gaussian conditional paths. Diffusion is thus recovered, approximately, as a special case of a broader framework in which the path can be chosen freely.

The simplest Gaussian conditional path moves each noise sample along a straight line to the data point, at constant speed. Its velocity is the difference between the data point and the noise sample, making the regression target easy to compute. This completes the central construction of flow matching: we can learn a velocity field directly, without learning a score or solving an ODE during training, using regression targets that are available in closed form.

However, simple conditional paths do not guarantee simple marginal trajectories. Even when every conditional trajectory is straight, the learned marginal trajectories can still curve. Noise and data points are also paired independently, and the source distribution remains Gaussian. Flow matching therefore solves the problem of learning velocity directly, but not yet the problem of making the resulting flow maximally efficient to sample.

The next post builds on this foundation to address these remaining limitations by exploring straighter marginal trajectories, better endpoint pairings, and more flexible source distributions.

The presentation of flows, flow models and flow matching in Parts 3 to 6 follows Holderrieth and Erives’s MIT lecture notes [10], and Lipman et al.’s guide covers the same ground with code [11].

Roadmap

  • Part 1: Sets out the limits of the diffusion models of post #3 that led to flow matching, traces flow models to fluid mechanics, and places the landmark papers in a lineage diagram.
  • Part 2: Develops normalizing flows, from the change of variables to planar flows, coupling layers and residual flows, and the determinant that restricts them.
  • Part 3: Introduces flows and the ODEs behind them and defines flow models, which Chen et al. call continuous normalizing flows. It samples from them with the Euler method, computes their exact likelihood and trains them by maximum likelihood, through FFJORD and RNODE, and ends with the two pitfalls of that training.
  • Part 4: Builds paths of distributions from noise to data and the velocity fields that follow them, and proves through the continuity equation that one of these fields carries noise to data.
  • Part 5: Starts from the probability-flow ODE, the first flow model trained without solving its ODE, and defines the flow-matching objective and conditional flow matching, the device that makes it tractable.
  • Part 6: Develops the paths that Lipman et al. train on, which are Gaussian at each time, with the diffusion paths and the path whose mean and standard deviation change linearly as two instances, and ends with three pitfalls that these paths keep.
  • Part 7: Summarizes how flow matching learns the velocity field directly and which pitfalls remain, and previews post #5.

1 From Diffusion Models to Flow Models

This Part starts where post #3 stopped, at the SDE framework of Song et al. [12]. It sets out the limits of that framework that led to flow matching (§1.1), traces flow models to their origin in fluid mechanics (§1.2), and draws the lineage of the landmark papers (§1.3).

1.1 The limits of diffusion models

Diffusion models in the SDE framework of Song et al. generate high-quality samples, but four limitations motivated flow matching:

  • Slow sampling: A sample needs hundreds to thousands of network evaluations.
  • Curved and uneven trajectories: The trajectories a sampler follows bend and change speed, which enlarges the error of each solver step.
  • A fixed probability path: The forward SDE fixes the path of distributions that generation follows, so it cannot be chosen.
  • A restricted source distribution: Generation starts from a Gaussian, so the model cannot carry one data distribution to another.

Lipman et al. [7] and Liu et al. [8] identify these limitations in the introductions to their papers.

Flow matching keeps the regression training of diffusion models, which never solves an ODE, and addresses the four limitations:

  • Straighter trajectories and faster sampling (Part 6 and post #5): Straight segments between noise and data, and better pairings of the two, reduce the curvature of the trajectories, so generation needs fewer steps.
  • Flexible probability paths (Parts 4–6): The path between the source and target distributions becomes a design choice rather than being fixed by the forward SDE.
  • Flexible source distributions (post #5): The source can be any distribution, not only a Gaussian.

1.1.1 Slow sampling

A diffusion model generates a sample by solving the reverse-time SDE or the probability-flow ODE step by step, and each step evaluates the network once. Many steps are needed. Song et al.’s samplers use 1,000 to 2,000 evaluations per sample on CIFAR-10, a dataset of 32 \times 32 colour images [12]. The probability-flow ODE needs fewer, because an adaptive solver takes larger steps where the solution changes slowly. On 256 \times 256 face images it used 14 evaluations at a higher error tolerance and 548 at a lower one (Song et al.’s Figure 3).

Liu et al. identify the computational cost of inference as a key drawback of continuous-time models compared with generators that transform noise into data in a single evaluation [8]. Specialized samplers such as denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIM) [13] and DPM-Solver [14] reduce the number of evaluations [7].

1.1.2 Curved and uneven trajectories

How many steps a solver needs depends on the shape of the trajectories it follows. Each step of the Euler method [15] follows the velocity at the start of the step, so the step is exact only when that velocity stays fixed, that is, when the trajectory is a straight line traversed at constant speed. The more a trajectory bends or changes speed, the larger the error of each step, and the more steps a sampler needs to keep the error small.

Diffusion paths fall short of this. On the path of the VP SDE, the default for diffusion models, a noisy sample is a weighted sum of a data point and a noise sample, with weights whose squares sum to one, so with the data point and the noise sample held fixed its trajectory is an arc. On the path of the VE SDE the corresponding trajectory is a straight segment, but its speed changes over time.

Lipman et al. contrast these paths with the straight, constant-speed trajectories of an optimal-transport path [7], named after optimal transport, the least-cost way to rearrange one distribution into another [16], [17]. §6.4 draws the VP and optimal-transport trajectories side by side, and P5:§4.4 bounds the error of one Euler step by the trajectory’s acceleration.

A sampler, however, follows a velocity field that averages, at each point, the velocities of the trajectories through it, so its own trajectories bend even on the optimal-transport path (§6.5.1). They bend less there than on the VP path [8].

1.1.3 A fixed probability path

A diffusion model chooses its path of distributions by choosing a perturbation kernel from a short list, such as those of the VP, VE and sub-VP SDEs, and then learns the score along that path. Lipman et al. call this a confined space of probability paths, narrower than the range a flow can follow, and link it to very long training times and to the need for the specialized samplers above [7].

The path also reaches noise only in the limit. At the terminal time T the VP marginal still depends on the data, because the weight of the data in the VP perturbation kernel is small but not zero, so generation starts from \mathcal{N}(0, I), which is close to the terminal marginal but not equal to it [7].

The path is not the only choice made by hand. The weighting of the training loss over time, the cutoff near the data and the sampler are chosen too, and Karras et al. separated these choices and tuned each on its own [18]. Citing that study, Liu et al. still describe the design space of diffusion models as involved and poorly understood [8].

1.1.4 A restricted source distribution

The forward SDE carries each data distribution close to one fixed Gaussian, so a diffusion model generates only from noise. Carrying one data distribution to another, as image-to-image translation requires, needs separate constructions. Liu et al. note that generative modeling and domain transfer were treated as separate problems, and pose both as one problem of transporting one distribution to another [8].

1.2 The origin of flow models

Flow models derive both their name and their mathematics from fluid mechanics. Euler described a moving fluid by its velocity at each point and each time [4]. Each particle of the fluid follows that velocity, so its trajectory is determined by where it starts, and Euler wrote the position of each particle as a function of its starting point and of time [19]. Because the fluid’s mass is neither created nor destroyed, its density and its velocity obey a single partial differential equation, which Euler also derived, the continuity equation [4].

Probability behaves the same way. A cloud of samples is a fluid whose mass is probability, so a velocity field that moves each sample also moves the whole distribution, and the continuity equation describes how its density changes. A generative model of this form is a velocity field that carries a simple distribution, such as a Gaussian, into the data distribution. Following a noise sample from start to end then turns it into a data sample. The probability-flow ODE of post #3 is already a model of this kind, with a velocity field built from the score.

In machine learning, flow models arrived along two routes: normalizing flows for density estimation, which Chen et al. made continuous, and the probability-flow ODE of diffusion. The landmarks below follow both.

1.3 Landmark papers

The papers this post and post #5 develop descend from two independent lines of work, normalizing flows and diffusion models, rather than from a single chain. The two lines meet in three methods of 2023, and three branches grow from those methods. Figure 1 below draws these dependencies, with each line running from a work to one that builds on it.

In the left column, Tabak and Turner [2], building on Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden [1], composed invertible maps into a normalizing flow, whose density stays exact because the change of variables tracks it through each map. Rezende and Mohamed used such flows for variational inference [20]. Each map must have a Jacobian determinant that is inexpensive to compute, since the change of variables evaluates one for each map, and this restricts the maps that can be used.

Chen et al. removed this restriction by letting a neural network define the velocity field of an ODE, so that a trace replaces the determinant [3]. Training such a flow model by maximum likelihood, however, solves the ODE at each step.

In the right column, Song et al. gave the SDE of each diffusion model a deterministic counterpart, an ODE whose velocity field is built from the score and whose solution has the marginals of the SDE’s solution, and named it the probability-flow ODE [12]. They credit the idea to Maoutsa et al., who simulated such ODEs with interacting particles and estimated the score by score matching [21]. Because denoising score matching (DSM) learns the score by regression, the velocity field of the probability-flow ODE is trained without solving the ODE, but only along the path that the forward SDE fixes.

De Bortoli et al. then used repeated diffusion training to solve the Schrödinger bridge problem [22], [23], the entropic form of optimal transport between two distributions [24].

The three methods of 2023 draw on both columns. The flows contribute the flow model, an ODE whose velocity field is a network, and diffusion contributes training by regression, which never solves the ODE. What the methods add is the freedom to choose the path.

Lipman et al. regress onto the velocity field of a probability path built from Gaussian conditional paths [7], Liu et al. onto the velocity along straight segments between paired points [8], and Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden onto the velocity field of an interpolant between the two distributions [9]. Liu et al. call their method rectified flow, and Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden call the interpolant a stochastic interpolant. The three were posted independently within a month of one another in 2022 and published in 2023, as the dashed line marks.

Three branches grow from the 2023 methods. Albergo, Boffi and Vanden-Eijnden extended stochastic interpolants with a Gaussian latent term into a framework that learns a velocity field and a score together, and so unifies flows with diffusion [25]. Pooladian et al. [26] and Tong et al. [27] kept flow matching but paired noise with data by solving an optimal-transport problem within each minibatch, which straightens the learned flow. Shi et al. returned to the Schrödinger bridge of De Bortoli et al. and solved it by bridge matching, which recovers rectified flow in the limit of zero noise [28].

The post also relies on classical results that it states, and at most sketches, without developing them. The change of variables is due to Euler [29], Lagrange [30] and Jacobi [31], the existence and uniqueness of ODE solutions to Picard [32] and Lindelöf [33], the stochastic trace estimator to Girard [34] and Hutchinson [35], the fixed-point theorem for contractions to Banach [36], and the mimicking theorem to Gyöngy [37].

Benamou and Brenier’s dynamic form of optimal transport [38] and the optimality of the conditional flow of the optimal-transport path [39] are stated where the post names them, and post #5 develops both.

2 Normalizing Flows

A normalizing flow carries a simple density, such as a Gaussian, through a sequence of invertible maps, and the change of variables tracks the density through each map, so the result is again a valid density with an exact likelihood [1], [2]. The name refers to the inverse direction, in which the flow normalizes the data by mapping it to a Gaussian, and goes back to Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden [1], and Rezende and Mohamed brought the construction to variational inference [20].

This Part states the change of variables (§2.1) and applies it to a sequence of maps, where the log-density of the result needs one Jacobian determinant per map (§2.2). Planar flows and coupling layers make that determinant inexpensive to compute, and residual flows replace its logarithm by a series. The Part ends with the restrictions those layers impose (§2.3).

2.1 Pushforward and change of variables

Each map of a normalizing flow transforms a sample, and the density of the result follows from the density of the sample. For a density p: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), a map f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d and a random point X \sim p, the pushforward f_\# p is the distribution of Y = f(X), with density p_Y: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty). The change of variables, which Euler [29] and Lagrange [30] derived in two and three dimensions and Jacobi [31] in general, gives its density when f is invertible and differentiable with a differentiable inverse,

\boxed{p_Y(y) = (f_\# p)(y) = p\big(f^{-1}(y)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial y}(y) \Big\rvert} \tag{1}

The determinant measures how f^{-1} scales volume near y, and so it corrects the density for the change of volume that f applies. Where f expands a region, the same probability spreads over a larger volume, and the density falls by the same factor.

2.2 Normalizing flows

Let f_1, \ldots, f_K: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d be invertible and differentiable with differentiable inverses, h_0 \sim p^{(0)} a sample of a simple base density p^{(0)}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), such as that of \mathcal{N}(0, I), and h_k = f_k(h_{k-1}) for k = 1, \ldots, K, with density p^{(k)}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), so that h_K = f_K \circ \cdots \circ f_1(h_0).

Since h_{k-1} \sim p^{(k-1)}, the change of variables Eq. 1 with f = f_k and p = p^{(k-1)} gives the density of h_k at y = h_k,

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}\big(f_k^{-1}(h_k)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k^{-1}}{\partial h}(h_k) \Big\rvert

Substituting f_k^{-1}(h_k) = h_{k-1},

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k^{-1}}{\partial h}(h_k) \Big\rvert

By the inverse function theorem, the Jacobian of f_k^{-1} at h_k is the inverse of the Jacobian of f_k at h_{k-1},

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \Big(\frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1})\Big)^{-1} \Big\rvert

Since the determinant of an inverse matrix is the reciprocal of its determinant,

p^{(k)}(h_k) = p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1})\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert^{-1}

Taking logarithms,

\log p^{(k)}(h_k) = \log p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1}) - \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert

Summing over k = 1, \ldots, K,

\sum_{k=1}^{K} \log p^{(k)}(h_k) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log p^{(k-1)}(h_{k-1}) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert

Telescoping, the intermediate log-densities cancel [20],

\boxed{\log p^{(K)}(h_K) = \log p^{(0)}(h_0) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial h}(h_{k-1}) \Big\rvert} \tag{2}

\square

Evaluating Eq. 2 requires the determinant of a d \times d Jacobian for each layer, which costs O(d^3) operations for a general map, about 3 \times 10^{10} for one layer on a 32 \times 32 colour image (d = 3072).

2.2.1 Planar flows

Rezende and Mohamed built the planar layer so that its Jacobian determinant is inexpensive to compute [20]. It is the map

f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad h \mapsto h + u \tanh(w^\top h + b)

with parameters u, w \in \mathbb{R}^d and b \in \mathbb{R} learned in training. The vector w and the offset b define the hyperplane w^\top h + b = 0, and the layer displaces each point h along the direction u, by the amount \tanh(w^\top h + b), which depends on the side of the hyperplane on which h lies and on its distance from it, so the layer expands or contracts the density in a band around that hyperplane. A normalizing flow built from planar layers is a planar flow.

Differentiating f with respect to h by the chain rule,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = I + u\, \tanh'(w^\top h + b)\, w^\top

Writing \psi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, h \mapsto \tanh'(w^\top h + b)\, w, the Jacobian is a rank-one update of the identity,

\frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = I + u\, \psi(h)^\top

Taking the determinant,

\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = \det\big(I + u\, \psi(h)^\top\big)

The matrix determinant lemma states that \det(I + a\, b^\top) = 1 + a^\top b for a, b \in \mathbb{R}^d. It holds because a\, b^\top has rank at most one, so 0 is its eigenvalue with multiplicity at least d - 1 and its remaining eigenvalue is its trace b^\top a; the eigenvalues of I + a\, b^\top are therefore 1, d - 1 times, and 1 + b^\top a, and the determinant is their product. Applying the lemma with a = u and b = \psi(h),

\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial h}(h) = 1 + u^\top \psi(h)

which costs O(d) operations instead of O(d^3).

The rank-one structure that makes the determinant inexpensive also limits the layer. It acts like a network with a single hidden unit, so each layer changes the density along one direction only. It is invertible only when w^\top u \ge -1 [20], and it has no inverse in closed form.

The lack of a closed-form inverse decides what a planar flow can be used for. Eq. 2 gives \log p^{(K)} at a point h_K through the points h_0, \ldots, h_{K-1} that lead to it. For a sample the flow generates, those points are computed on the way forward, from h_0 \sim p^{(0)} through each layer, so Eq. 2 needs no inverse. For a given x \in \mathbb{R}^d, such as a training image, only h_K = x is known. Recovering h_{K-1} = f_K^{-1}(x), and so on back to h_0, needs the inverse of each layer, which for a planar layer means solving a scalar equation for w^\top h numerically [20].

Planar flows therefore suit variational inference, which fits a flow to an intractable target distribution, such as a Bayesian posterior, using the flow’s own samples, their densities and the unnormalized target density. They do not suit training on data, which needs the density at each training image and so a numerical solve for each layer at each training step [5], [20].

A few planar layers already turn a Gaussian into a density with several modes. Because Eq. 2 runs forward, plotting the density p^{(k)} after k layers needs no inverse either. A fine grid of base points h_0 is pushed through the first k layers, and Eq. 2 gives \log p^{(k)} at each image h_k. Figure 2 below shows the result for four planar layers in two dimensions, each with w^\top u > -1, a condition that makes the layer invertible with a differentiable inverse [20].

The determinant 1 + u^\top \psi(h) = 1 + (w^\top u)\, \tanh'(w^\top h + b) explains each panel. The first two layers have w^\top u = 3.9, so the determinant exceeds one near the line w^\top h + b = 0, where \tanh' is largest, and reaches 4.9 on the line itself. The density is divided by the determinant, so it drops along that line. A trough opens along the vertical axis and splits the Gaussian into two modes, and a second trough along the horizontal axis splits them into four. The last two layers have w^\top u = 0, so their determinant is one. They preserve volume and only shear the four modes along lines parallel to the two diagonals.

2.2.2 Coupling layers

A coupling layer splits its input into two halves, keeps one and updates the other by an invertible map whose parameters depend on the kept half. Coupling layers have an inverse in closed form, so a flow built from them can be trained on data by maximum likelihood.

Dinh et al. introduced them on arXiv in 2014, before planar flows, in Non-linear Independent Components Estimation (NICE) [40]. NICE splits h into two halves h_a, h_b \in \mathbb{R}^{d/2}, keeps h_a and replaces h_b by h_b + m(h_a), where m: \mathbb{R}^{d/2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d/2} is an arbitrary network. Because h_a passes through unchanged, subtracting m(h_a) undoes the update, so the inverse costs as much as the map itself. Its Jacobian is triangular with ones on the diagonal, so its determinant is one.

The real-valued non-volume-preserving (RealNVP) layer makes the update affine. It replaces h_b by h_b \odot \exp\big(s(h_a)\big) + t(h_a) with networks s, t: \mathbb{R}^{d/2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d/2} and \odot the elementwise product [41]. Its Jacobian is triangular, so its log-determinant is the sum of the entries of s(h_a). Glow inserts a learned invertible 1 \times 1 convolution, one linear map applied to the channels of each pixel, between coupling layers to mix the two halves. Writing its matrix as a permutation times triangular matrices (an LU factorization) makes the determinant, up to sign, the product of their diagonal entries [42].

These layers trained flows by maximum likelihood on images. On CIFAR-10, RealNVP [41] reaches 3.49 and Glow [42] 3.35 bits per dimension, the negative log-likelihood -\log_2 p(x)/d of a test image averaged over the test set, where lower is better. Since a density depends on the scale of x, these figures use the pixel values, integers from 0 to 255, made continuous by adding uniform noise on [0, 1).

2.2.3 Residual flows

A residual layer f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, h \mapsto h + g(h), adds the output of a differentiable network g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d to its input, as in the residual networks of He et al. [43]. Behrmann et al. showed that a general network can serve as g in a flow when g is a contraction, a map with \lVert g(h) - g(h') \rVert \le L\, \lVert h - h' \rVert for each pair of points and a constant L < 1 [44].

They build g from linear maps and from nonlinearities that increase no distance, and keep L below one by keeping the operator norm \lVert W \rVert of each weight matrix W, the largest factor by which W stretches the length of a vector, below one. They rescale W to c\, W / \hat s whenever \hat s > c, where \hat s is an estimate of \lVert W \rVert and c < 1 is a chosen coefficient. This is a variant of the spectral normalization of Miyato et al. [45].

The layer is then invertible. For each y \in \mathbb{R}^d the map h \mapsto y - g(h) is a contraction with the same constant L, so by Banach’s fixed-point theorem it has exactly one fixed point, and the iteration h \leftarrow y - g(h) converges to it from each starting point [36]. The fixed point satisfies h + g(h) = y, so it is f^{-1}(y), and the iteration computes the inverse.

The log-determinant has a power series instead of a closed form. The Jacobian of the layer is I + J_g, with J_g = \frac{\partial g}{\partial h}(h) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} the Jacobian of g. Its operator norm \lVert J_g \rVert is at most L, since for each a \in \mathbb{R}^d the vector J_g a is the limit of \big(g(h + \varepsilon a) - g(h)\big)/\varepsilon as \varepsilon \to 0, whose length the contraction bounds by L\, \lVert a \rVert. An eigenvector is stretched by the modulus of its eigenvalue, so the eigenvalues \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_d of J_g, counted with multiplicity, satisfy \lvert \lambda_j \rvert \le L < 1.

The eigenvalues 1 + \lambda_j of I + J_g therefore have positive real parts. The real ones are positive, and the others come in conjugate pairs whose products \lvert 1 + \lambda_j \rvert^2 are positive, so the determinant, the product of the eigenvalues, is positive. The principal logarithms \log(1 + \lambda_j), those with imaginary part in (-\pi, \pi), of a conjugate pair are conjugate, so their imaginary parts cancel in the sum. Taking the logarithm of the product,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \log(1 + \lambda_j)

Expanding each logarithm in its power series, which converges since \lvert \lambda_j \rvert < 1,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \lambda_j^k

Exchanging the two sums, which converge absolutely,

\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{d} \lambda_j^k

Since the eigenvalues of J_g^k are the \lambda_j^k, whose sum is its trace,

\boxed{\log \det\big(I + J_g\big) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \operatorname{tr}\big(J_g^k\big)} \tag{3}

\square

Behrmann et al. truncate the series after a fixed number of terms and estimate each trace stochastically, from products of the Jacobian with random vectors, each of which costs about as much as evaluating g, so no d \times d determinant is formed. The truncation biases the estimate. The residual flows of Chen, Behrmann, Duvenaud and Jacobsen remove the bias by truncating at a random number of terms and reweighting the terms that remain [46]. A general network as g thus comes with two requirements, the contraction constraint on each layer and an inverse computed by iteration rather than by a formula.

2.3 Pitfalls

Normalizing flows built from a finite sequence of maps give exact likelihoods, or, with residual layers, estimates of them, but the determinant in Eq. 2 restricts them in two ways.

2.3.1 Restricted architectures

Each map must have a Jacobian whose determinant is inexpensive to compute, such as a rank-one update of the identity or a triangular matrix, so a general network cannot serve as a layer [5]. Chen et al. name this restriction as their reason to make flows continuous [3]. Residual layers, which came later, admit a general network only as a contraction, and their log-determinant is then a series that must be estimated (§2.2.3).

2.3.2 Deep stacks

To keep its Jacobian triangular, each coupling layer applies only an elementwise affine update to half the coordinates, conditioned on the other half. Two alternating layers already transform each coordinate [40], but a flow needs many such layers to be expressive. Glow uses 3 levels of 32 steps on CIFAR-10, each step a coupling layer with its 1 \times 1 convolution and a normalization, and 5 levels of 64 steps on 128 \times 128 images [42], and memory limits such deep stacks at high resolution [41], [42].

3 Flow Models

Flow models remove the pitfalls of Part 2 by replacing the sequence of maps with the flow of an ODE, along whose trajectories the log-density of the transported distribution changes by a trace instead of a determinant [3].

This Part defines trajectories, velocity fields, ODEs and their flows, which the vortex of a viscous fluid illustrates, and flow models, whose velocity field is computed by a neural network and whose distributions form a probability path. It samples from a flow model with the Euler method, derives the model’s exact likelihood and relates it to the residual layers of Part 2, and trains the model by maximum likelihood with the adjoint method. It then presents FFJORD and RNODE, which lowered the cost of that training, and the two pitfalls that remain.

3.1 ODEs and flows

An ODE describes how a point moves through space over time, and three objects make this precise. All three come from Euler’s mechanics of fluids, which describes a fluid by its velocity field over space [4] and by the trajectories of its particles as functions of their initial positions and time, the flow below [19]. Lie later studied the maps that a velocity field fixed in time generates as a group of transformations [47].

Trajectory (X_t): A function that assigns a position in space \mathbb{R}^d to each time,

X: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad t \mapsto X_t

Velocity field (v_t(x)): A function that assigns a velocity, a vector in \mathbb{R}^d, to each point of space at each time,

v: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto v_t(x)

An ODE requires a trajectory X to start at an initial condition x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d and to have, at each time t, the velocity v_t(X_t) of the point it occupies. A trajectory that meets both requirements is a solution of the ODE,

\boxed{X_0 = x_0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t)} \tag{4}

Flow (\phi_t(x)): The trajectories that solve the ODE Eq. 4, as a function of the initial condition and the time,

\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto \phi_t(x)

whose value \phi_t(x_0) is the position at time t of the trajectory X with the initial condition X_0 = x_0. Substituting X_t = \phi_t(x_0) into Eq. 4, the flow \phi_t(x_0) solves

\boxed{\phi_0(x_0) = x_0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0) = v_t\big(\phi_t(x_0)\big)} \tag{5}

for each initial condition x_0. By the Picard-Lindelöf theorem [32], [33], [48], the flow \phi_t(x) exists and is unique on [0, 1] when v_t(x) is continuous in t and Lipschitz [49] in x uniformly in t, that is, when \lVert v_t(x) - v_t(y) \rVert \le K\, \lVert x - y \rVert \forall\, x, y \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in [0, 1] for some constant K.

3.1.1 Lamb-Oseen vortex: an example of a flow

Fluid dynamics gives these objects a direct physical meaning. In a moving fluid the velocity field v_t(x) is the fluid’s velocity at each point x, a trajectory X is the path of one fluid particle, and the flow \phi_t(x) carries each particle from its position x at t = 0 to its position at time t.

Here we draw the flow \phi_t(x) of a Lamb-Oseen vortex [50], [51], [52], the standard model of a viscous vortex such as a whirlpool. The fluid circles the origin counterclockwise, and at distance r from the origin its angular speed is

\omega: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty), \qquad r \mapsto \frac{\kappa}{r^2}\big(1 - e^{-r^2/r_c^2}\big)

where \kappa > 0 sets the vortex’s strength and r_c is the radius of its core, which we hold fixed. In Cartesian coordinates its velocity field is v_t(x) = \omega(\lVert x \rVert)\, R\, x for x \neq 0 and v_t(0) = 0, the same at each time t, with R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} the counterclockwise rotation by a right angle.

In polar coordinates (r, \vartheta), the trajectory (r_t, \vartheta_t) of a fluid particle of the Lamb-Oseen vortex solves the ODE,

(r_0, \vartheta_0) = (r, \vartheta), \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, (r_t, \vartheta_t) = \big(0,\ \omega(r_t)\big)

Since \frac{d}{dt}\, r_t = 0, the radius stays r_t = r and the angle grows at the constant rate \omega(r), so the solution of this ODE is the flow, in polar coordinates,

\phi_t(r, \vartheta) = \big(r,\ \vartheta + \omega(r)\, t\big)

which rotates a particle at a distance r from the origin by the angle \omega(r)\, t in time t while keeping the distance from the origin fixed.

Figure 3 below shows the flow as a deformed square grid, a device of D’Arcy Thompson [53]. The grid is made of fluid particles. It starts as a square at t = 0, and the flow deforms it as time passes. Each panel shows where the grid is at time t, which is \phi_t(x) for each point x of the initial grid. The arrows are the fluid velocity v_t(x) at the points x of a fixed lattice, the same in each panel.

Particles near the core turn faster than those farther out, so the straight grid lines wind into a spiral that is tightest at the core.

In Figure 4 below, we follow fluid particles, drawn as dots, through the same vortex for t \in [0, 1]. Each dot carries an arrow along the fluid velocity v_t(x) at its position x, which is tangent to the circle the particle travels on and proportional in length to its speed.

Each dot moves along its arrow, and the arrow stays tangent to the dot’s circle about the origin as the dot circles it. Near the center the angular speed is almost constant, \omega(r) \approx \kappa / r_c^2, so the dots there turn together like points of a rigid disk and keep their arrangement. Farther out the angular speed falls off with distance, so the inner dots pull ahead of the outer ones and the initial lattice winds into a spiral. The speed \omega(r)\, r peaks at r \approx 1.12\, r_c, just outside the core, where the arrows are longest, and decays like \kappa / r beyond it.

3.2 Generation using flow models

This section builds a generative model from the ODE of §3.1 by learning its velocity field [3]. The field is learned so that a point sampled at t = 0 from a simple initial distribution, independent of the data distribution, follows the field to a point at t = 1 that is a random sample from the data distribution.

Chen et al. combined two earlier ideas. Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden had estimated densities with a map built as a flow that carries the samples toward a Gaussian [1]. E proposed treating deep networks as dynamical systems [54], and Lu et al. [55], Haber and Ruthotto [56], and Ruthotto and Haber [57] viewed residual networks as Euler steps of an ODE.

3.2.1 Definitions

The generative model built here has no forward process to reverse, so its time axis runs in the generative direction, from noise at t = 0 to data at t = 1, whereas the rest of the series has t = 0 as data. The model uses these objects, besides the trajectory X, velocity field v_t(x) and flow \phi_t(x) of §3.1.

  • Initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}: A simple distribution on \mathbb{R}^d, such as \mathcal{N}(0, I), from which the initial condition is sampled, with density p_{\mathrm{init}}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty).
  • Data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}: The distribution on \mathbb{R}^d that generated samples should follow, with density p_{\mathrm{data}}: \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty).
  • Probability path p_t: A probability distribution on \mathbb{R}^d for each time t \in [0, 1], with a density for each t \in [0, 1); the distribution at t = 1 may be concentrated at one point and then has no density. At a fixed x \in \mathbb{R}^d, the path gives how the density at x changes over time, p: [0, 1) \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), \qquad (t, x) \mapsto p_t(x)
  • Parameters \theta: The weights of a neural network.
  • Network velocity field v_\theta(x, t): The velocity field the network represents, v_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad (x, t) \mapsto v_\theta(x, t)
  • Flow \phi^\theta_t(x): The flow of v_\theta(x, t), \phi^\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto \phi^\theta_t(x), with \phi^\theta_t(x_0) the position at time t of the trajectory of v_\theta(x, t) with the initial condition X_0 = x_0.

3.2.2 Flow model

Generated samples must be random, but the solution of an ODE is deterministic for a given initial condition. The randomness therefore enters through the initial condition, sampled from p_{\mathrm{init}}. A flow model is the ODE Eq. 4 with this random initial condition X_0 and the network velocity field v_\theta(x, t),

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_\theta(X_t, t)} \tag{6}

The model is trained to make its solution at t = 1 follow the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}},

X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \phi^\theta_1(X_0) \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}

so that solving the ODE from the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} produces a sample of p_{\mathrm{data}}. The distribution p^\theta_t of X_t, a probability path p^\theta: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), (t, x) \mapsto p^\theta_t(x), starts at p^\theta_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}, so the learned field v_\theta(x, t) transports the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} along a path of intermediate marginals p^\theta_t, ending at p_{\mathrm{data}}.

Since X_t = \phi^\theta_t(X_0), the distribution p^\theta_t is the pushforward (§2.1) of p_{\mathrm{init}} under the flow, the distribution of \phi^\theta_t(x) for x \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, written p^\theta_t = (\phi^\theta_t)_\# p_{\mathrm{init}}. For a velocity field that is continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz as in the Picard-Lindelöf theorem above, the flow is invertible, since solving the ODE backward inverts it. The flow and its inverse are also differentiable in x, because the solution of an ODE with a continuously differentiable velocity field depends differentiably on its initial condition [48], [58]. So Eq. 1 gives the density of the pushforward,

p^\theta_t(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}\big((\phi^\theta_t)^{-1}(x)\big)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial (\phi^\theta_t)^{-1}}{\partial x}(x) \Big\rvert

Chen et al. call this model a continuous normalizing flow [3], and Lipman et al. state flow matching in these terms [7].

The network computes the velocity field v_\theta(x, t) and never the flow \phi^\theta_t(x) that names the model, so producing a sample requires solving the ODE numerically (§3.3).

3.3 Sampling with the Euler method

A flow model generates a sample by solving Eq. 6 from the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and returning X_1. The ODE is solved numerically, and the simplest scheme is the Euler method [15], which replaces the derivative in Eq. 6 by a forward difference over a step \Delta t. On the grid t_i = i\, \Delta t with \Delta t = 1/n, and with x_i the approximation of X_{t_i}, sampling runs as follows.

Algorithm 7 — Sampling from a flow model with the Euler method [15]:

1: x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}
2: for i = 0, \ldots, n - 1 do
    3: x_{i+1} = x_i + v_\theta(x_i, t_i)\, \Delta t
4: end for
5: return x_n

Each step moves the sample along the network velocity field v_\theta(x, t) for a time \Delta t, and the returned x_n approximates X_1 = \phi^\theta_1(x_0), a sample of the model’s distribution p^\theta_1.

3.4 Exact likelihood via the instantaneous change of variables

A flow model also gives the exact likelihood of each point, which the stochastic samplers of the reverse-time SDE cannot. The likelihood comes from the instantaneous change of variables, the continuous-time form of the change of variables Eq. 1. Along each trajectory of a velocity field v_t(x), the log-density of the pushforward p_t = (\phi_t)_\# p_0 changes at the rate -\nabla_x \cdot v_t. This rate follows from Euler’s equation for the density of a moving fluid [4], and Chen et al. named the result and used it to compute likelihoods [3]. The derivation below applies Eq. 1 to the flow \phi_t and differentiates the result in time.

We assume that v_t(x) is continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz, as in §3.2.2, and that p_0 > 0. Applying Eq. 1 with f = \phi_t, p = p_0 and y = \phi_t(x), so that f^{-1}(y) = x,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \Big\lvert \det \frac{\partial \phi_t^{-1}}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big) \Big\rvert

By the inverse function theorem, the Jacobian of \phi_t^{-1} at \phi_t(x) is the inverse of the Jacobian J_t(x) = \frac{\partial \phi_t}{\partial x}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} of \phi_t at x,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \big\lvert \det J_t(x)^{-1} \big\rvert

Since the determinant of an inverse matrix is the reciprocal of its determinant,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = p_0(x)\, \big\lvert \det J_t(x) \big\rvert^{-1}

The determinant \det J_t(x) equals \det I = 1 at t = 0, depends continuously on t and never vanishes, because J_t(x) has an inverse, the Jacobian of \phi_t^{-1} at \phi_t(x), so it stays positive. Dropping the absolute value,

p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{p_0(x)}{\det J_t(x)}

Taking logarithms,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \log p_0(x) - \log \det J_t(x)

Differentiating in t, where p_0(x) does not depend on t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\frac{d}{dt}\, \log \det J_t(x)

By Jacobi’s formula for the derivative of a determinant [59], \frac{d}{dt} \log \det J = \operatorname{tr}\big(J^{-1}\, \frac{d}{dt} J\big),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(J_t(x)^{-1}\, \frac{d}{dt} J_t(x)\Big)

Differentiating the flow ODE Eq. 5 with respect to x, by the chain rule, shows that the Jacobian evolves as \frac{d}{dt} J_t(x) = \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x). Substituting it,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(J_t(x)^{-1}\, \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x)\Big)

By the cyclic property of the trace, \operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(BCA),

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\, J_t(x)\, J_t(x)^{-1}\Big)

Since J_t(x)\, J_t(x)^{-1} = I,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -\operatorname{tr}\Big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)\Big)

Since the trace of the Jacobian of v_t is its divergence, \operatorname{tr}\big(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{\partial v_t^{j}}{\partial x^{j}} = \nabla_x \cdot v_t, with x^j and v_t^j the j-th coordinates of x and v_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Integrating both sides from 0 to t, with s as the integration variable,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) - \log p_0\big(\phi_0(x)\big) = -\int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds

Since \phi_0(x) = x by Eq. 5,

\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) - \log p_0(x) = -\int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds

Adding \log p_0(x) to both sides,

\boxed{\log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \log p_0(x) - \int_0^t (\nabla_x \cdot v_s)\big(\phi_s(x)\big)\, ds} \tag{7}

\square

3.4.1 Exact likelihood of a flow model

For the flow model, p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}} and the velocity field is v_\theta, so Eq. 7 at t = 1 gives the exact log-likelihood of each point x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d [3]. Applying it with x = x_0, where x_0 = (\phi^\theta_1)^{-1}(x_1) is the point that \phi^\theta_1 maps to x_1,

\log p^\theta_1(x_1) = \log p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0) - \int_0^1 (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)\big(\phi^\theta_s(x_0),\, s\big)\, ds

Solving the flow ODE of v_\theta backward, from x_1 at t = 1 to t = 0, gives x_0, and the same solve accumulates the integral of the divergence along the trajectory.

Compared with Eq. 2, the continuous form differs in two respects [3].

  • A trace instead of a determinant: The sum of log-determinants becomes the integral of a divergence, the trace of the Jacobian \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}. The trace needs only the d diagonal entries of that Jacobian, while a determinant costs O(d^3), so the velocity field needs no triangular Jacobian of the kind coupling layers build. The exact trace still costs d backward passes of reverse-mode automatic differentiation, one for each diagonal entry (P2:§3.3.3.4), a cost that §3.6 reduces.
  • No invertible building blocks: The flow needs no invertible maps as building blocks, since any velocity field that meets the Picard-Lindelöf conditions gives an invertible flow (§3.2.2).

The first difference appears in the discrete formula itself when its layers are small residual layers. One step of Algorithm 7, x \mapsto x + \Delta t\, v_\theta(x, t_i), is a residual layer (§2.2.3) with g = \Delta t\, v_\theta(\cdot, t_i), a contraction with the constant K\, \Delta t once K\, \Delta t < 1, where K is the Lipschitz constant of v_\theta, so that \lVert J_g \rVert \le K\, \Delta t as in §2.2.3. In Eq. 3, J_g = \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i), so its k-th term is of order \Delta t^k. Separating the first term, \operatorname{tr}(J_g) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i), from the others,

\log \det\Big(I + \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i)\Big) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i) + \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\, \operatorname{tr}\big(J_g^k\big)

Bounding the remaining terms by the geometric series d\, K^2 \Delta t^2 / (1 - K\, \Delta t), since \operatorname{tr}(J_g^k) is the sum of the d values \lambda_j^k of §2.2.3, each of modulus at most \lVert J_g \rVert^k \le (K\, \Delta t)^k,

\log \det\Big(I + \Delta t\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(x, t_i)\Big) = \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x, t_i) + O(\Delta t^2)

This bound is the same at each x and t_i, so the constant in O(\Delta t^2) is the same for each layer. The sum of the log-determinants of n = 1/\Delta t such layers in Eq. 2 is then the Riemann sum \sum_i \Delta t\, (\nabla_x \cdot v_\theta)(x_i, t_i) of the divergence at the layers’ inputs, up to n \cdot O(\Delta t^2) = O(\Delta t). The exact log-likelihood above has, in place of this sum, the integral of the divergence along the trajectory \phi^\theta_s(x_0), where the sum evaluates the divergence at the Euler iterates x_i.

3.5 Maximum-likelihood training and the adjoint method

Since Eq. 7 gives the exact log-likelihood \log p^\theta_1(x_1) of each point, Chen et al. train a flow model by maximum likelihood [3]. The parameters \theta maximize the average log-likelihood of the data,

\max_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\big[\log p^\theta_1(x_1)\big]

Each training step therefore evaluates \log p^\theta_1(x_1) for each x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} in a minibatch, by the backward solve of §3.4. Writing L_t = -\int_t^1 \nabla_x \cdot v_\theta(X_s, s)\, ds \in \mathbb{R} for the integral accumulated from t = 1 back to t, the trajectory and the integral solve one joint ODE [3], [5],

\frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_\theta(X_t, t), \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\, L_t = \nabla_x \cdot v_\theta(X_t, t), \qquad X_1 = x_1,\ L_1 = 0

Solving it from t = 1 back to t = 0 gives x_0 = X_0 and L_0, so \log p^\theta_1(x_1) = \log p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0) + L_0 by Eq. 7 at t = 1 for the flow model.

Backpropagating through the solver would store each of its internal steps, so the memory of a training step would grow with their number. The adjoint method computes the gradient with constant memory instead, by solving a second ODE from the end of the first solve back to its start. It comes from the optimal control of Pontryagin et al. [60], and Chen et al. brought it to neural ODEs, ODEs whose right-hand side is a neural network [3].

The method applies to any ODE \frac{d}{dt}\, Z_t = f(Z_t, t, \theta) with a state Z_t \in \mathbb{R}^m, parameters \theta \in \mathbb{R}^P and a right-hand side f: \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^m, (z, t, \theta) \mapsto f(z, t, \theta), solved from t_0 to t_1. The joint ODE above is one, with Z_t = (X_t, L_t), m = d + 1, t_0 = 1 and t_1 = 0. For a loss \mathcal{L} that depends on the final state Z_{t_1}, the adjoint is the row vector a(t) = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial Z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times m}, the sensitivity of the loss to the state at time t. Since \mathcal{L} depends on Z_t only through Z_{t+\varepsilon}, for a short step \varepsilon toward t_1, by the chain rule,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial Z_{t+\varepsilon}}{\partial Z_t}

Expanding the solution to first order in \varepsilon, Z_{t+\varepsilon} = Z_t + \varepsilon f(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2), and differentiating in Z_t gives the Jacobian of the step, \partial Z_{t+\varepsilon} / \partial Z_t = I + \varepsilon\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2). Substituting it,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon)\, \Big[I + \varepsilon\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)\Big]

Expanding the product,

a(t) = a(t + \varepsilon) + \varepsilon\, a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Moving a(t + \varepsilon) to the left-hand side,

a(t) - a(t + \varepsilon) = \varepsilon\, a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon^2)

Dividing by -\varepsilon,

\frac{a(t + \varepsilon) - a(t)}{\varepsilon} = -\,a(t + \varepsilon)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta) + O(\varepsilon)

Letting \varepsilon \to 0,

\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\, a(t) = -\,a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(Z_t, t, \theta)} \tag{8}

\square

The gradient with respect to \theta follows from the same argument, with \theta as a second state that does not change in time, \frac{d}{dt}\, \theta_t = 0 [3]. Its adjoint is the row vector a_\theta(t) = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times P}, the sensitivity of the loss to the value of \theta used from time t on. The augmented state (Z_t, \theta_t) has the right-hand side (f, 0), whose Jacobian is \begin{pmatrix} \partial f / \partial z & \partial f / \partial \theta \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. So the \theta-component of Eq. 8 for the augmented state is

\frac{d}{dt}\, a_\theta(t) = -\,a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)

Integrating from t_1 to t_0,

a_\theta(t_0) - a_\theta(t_1) = -\int_{t_1}^{t_0} a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)\, dt

The adjoint a_\theta starts at a_\theta(t_1) = 0, because no time is left after t_1 for \theta to act. It ends at a_\theta(t_0) = d\mathcal{L}/d\theta, because the value of \theta used from t_0 on is \theta itself. Substituting both values,

\boxed{\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta} = -\int_{t_1}^{t_0} a(t)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(Z_t, t, \theta)\, dt}

\square

3.5.1 The adjoint solve and its cost

The state Z_t, recomputed from its final value, and the adjoints a(t) and a_\theta(t) solve one joint ODE from t_1 back to t_0. It starts from Z_{t_1}, a(t_1) = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial Z_{t_1} and a_\theta(t_1) = 0 (Chen et al.’s Algorithm 1) [3]. The right-hand sides of the adjoint ODEs are vector-Jacobian products, a row vector times a Jacobian. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation computes each at about the cost of one evaluation of f.

This solve recomputes the state instead of storing the steps of the first solve, so the memory does not grow with the number of steps. The time does grow, since it is proportional to the number of function evaluations (NFE), the evaluations of f that a solve needs. Chen et al. use adaptive solvers, which choose their step sizes to meet an error tolerance, and in their experiments this number grew as training proceeded (their Figure 3d, for a classifier of MNIST, a dataset of 28 \times 28 images of handwritten digits).

3.6 Free-form flows: FFJORD

Grathwohl et al.’s Free-form Jacobian of Reversible Dynamics (FFJORD) replaces the exact divergence in Eq. 7 with a stochastic estimate [5]. Chen et al. had kept the cost of the exact divergence low by restricting the velocity field. They built it from sums of simple terms, each with a trace in closed form, and the trace of the sum is the sum of these traces [3].

The divergence is the trace of the d \times d Jacobian \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}, and computing it exactly costs the d backward passes of §3.4. The trace is also an expectation over a random probe \eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). For a constant matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, writing the scalar \eta^\top A\, \eta as its own trace and using the cyclic property of the trace,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{tr}(A\, \eta \eta^\top)\big]

Exchanging the trace and the expectation, both linear, with A constant,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \operatorname{tr}\big(A\, \mathbb{E}[\eta \eta^\top]\big)

Since \mathbb{E}[\eta \eta^\top] = I,

\mathbb{E}\big[\eta^\top A\, \eta\big] = \operatorname{tr}(A)

Applying it with A = \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(x), whose trace is \nabla_x \cdot v_t(x),

\nabla_x \cdot v_t(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\Big[\eta^\top\, \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}(x)\, \eta\Big]

The Hutchinson trace estimator [34], [35] replaces this expectation with its value at one sample of \eta. Each such value costs one backward pass, which computes the vector-Jacobian product \eta^\top \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial x}, and then a dot product with \eta. Grathwohl et al. brought the estimator to flow models [5], Behrmann et al. used it for the traces in Eq. 3, and it is the same single-probe technique that makes Song et al.’s sliced score matching inexpensive [61].

Holding one probe \eta fixed for each solve keeps the ODE deterministic, as an adaptive solver requires. The estimate of \log p^\theta_1(x_1) stays unbiased, since the expectation over \eta can be taken outside the time integral [5]. The cost of the divergence falls from d backward passes to one, which Grathwohl et al. state as O(d^2) against O(d) time, so the velocity field v_\theta can be any network.

FFJORD reached 0.99 bits per dimension on MNIST, ahead of Glow’s 1.05 with less than 2% of Glow’s parameters, and 3.40 on CIFAR-10, against Glow’s 3.35 [5]. Its image models took about five days to train on six graphics processing units (GPUs).

Grathwohl et al. name two limitations. The NFE “tends to grow as the models trains and can become prohibitively large”, and general-purpose solvers restrict the flow to non-stiff dynamics. A stiff ODE has components that change on time scales differing by orders of magnitude, and an explicit solver stays stable on it only with steps on the shortest of those scales.

3.7 Regularized flows: RNODE

Finlay et al. attributed the growing NFE to the learned velocity field itself [6]. The velocity field that maximizes the likelihood is not unique, because maximum likelihood constrains only the distribution at t = 1. Training can settle on a field whose trajectories turn sharply and change speed, which an adaptive solver follows only in small steps. Training FFJORD on CIFAR-10, they found the NFE strongly correlated with the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of v_\theta, the square root of the sum of its squared entries.

Their method, the regularized neural ODE (RNODE), adds two penalties to FFJORD’s negative log-likelihood [6]. The first is the kinetic energy, the integral of the squared speed \lVert v_\theta \rVert^2 along a trajectory. The second is the integral of the squared Frobenius norm of the Jacobian \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x} along it. With X_t the trajectory of v_\theta that ends at X_1 = x_1, and weights \lambda_K, \lambda_J > 0, the objective is

\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\Big[-\log p^\theta_1(x_1) + \lambda_K \int_0^1 \big\lVert v_\theta(X_s, s) \big\rVert^2\, ds + \lambda_J \int_0^1 \Big\lVert \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x}(X_s, s) \Big\rVert_F^2\, ds\Big]

The kinetic term favours trajectories that run in straight lines at constant speed. Among the velocity fields that carry one distribution to another, those of least kinetic energy have such trajectories, by the dynamic formulation of optimal transport that Benamou and Brenier introduced and post #5 develops [38]. The kinetic term straightens only the trajectories that the training data follow, however, which is one reason Finlay et al. add the Jacobian term.

The Jacobian term needs no extra backward pass. Its integrand is an expectation over the same probe \eta as the divergence estimate, since \lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A A^\top) = \mathbb{E}_{\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\lVert \eta^\top A \rVert^2. The vector-Jacobian product \eta^\top \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial x} it needs is the one that estimate already computes.

With \lambda_K = \lambda_J = 0.01, RNODE trained about 2.8 times faster than FFJORD on MNIST and on CIFAR-10, at comparable bits per dimension [6]. On CIFAR-10 it reached 3.38, against 3.36 for Finlay et al.’s own FFJORD run and 3.40 as Grathwohl et al. reported. It also trained on ImageNet, a dataset of about 1.3 million natural images, downsampled to 64 \times 64 pixels, reaching 3.83, where their FFJORD run failed to train.

3.8 Pitfalls

Maximum-likelihood training of flow models works, but it has two pitfalls, and flow matching, the subject of Parts 4 to 6, removes both.

3.8.1 Training solves the ODE

Each training step of §3.5 solves the ODE backward, from t = 1 to t = 0, for each x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} in the minibatch, and then solves the adjoint ODE from t = 0 back to t = 1. Both solves use an adaptive solver, whose NFE grows as training proceeds (§3.6). A training step therefore costs at least two solves of the ODE for each point of the minibatch, where generating a sample costs one. This cost is why FFJORD’s image models took days to train, and a stiff flow, which forces small steps, would raise it further.

3.8.2 The path is not specified

Maximum likelihood leaves the probability path from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p^\theta_1 to the optimizer, since the likelihood depends only on the distribution p^\theta_1 at t = 1 (§3.7). Many probability paths connect the same two distributions. Along each of them the velocity field is not unique either, since a field that moves mass without changing the intermediate distributions can be added, which Part 4 makes precise. The optimizer’s choice among them can be irregular.

Liu et al. call the maximum-likelihood problem for neural ODEs under-specified for this reason, as it leaves the paths “for the algorithm to figure out implicitly” [8]. RNODE’s penalties favour straighter paths but still leave the choice to the optimizer, whereas flow matching fixes the path before training.

4 Probability Paths and the Continuity Equation

Flow matching removes both pitfalls of §3.8. It fixes the path first, so the path is specified, and it trains by regression onto a velocity field constructed for the path, so training never solves the ODE.

Training seeks parameters \theta such that solving Eq. 6 with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} ends at X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. Flow matching [7], [8], [9] does it in three steps: fixing a probability path p_t from noise to data (§4.1), constructing a velocity field whose trajectories follow it (§4.2), and regressing the network onto that field (§5.2).

This Part carries out the first two steps. It defines conditional and marginal probability paths, with a Gaussian path to a spiral as the running example, and their conditional and marginal velocity fields.

The Part then states the continuity equation, proves that a probability path satisfies it with a velocity field if and only if the path is the distribution of that field’s ODE solution, and uses this to prove that the ODE solution of the marginal velocity field has the marginal path as its distribution. It ends by showing that the continuity equation does not determine the velocity field. Part 5 carries out the third step.

4.1 Conditional and marginal probability paths

A conditional probability path [7] is, for each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, a probability density at each time t \in [0, 1),

p_t(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), \qquad x \mapsto p_t(x \mid x_1), \qquad t \in [0, 1)

that starts at the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} and ends, at t = 1, concentrated at x_1,

\boxed{p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \delta(\cdot - x_1)} \tag{9}

The Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - a) [62] at a point a \in \mathbb{R}^d is the distribution that puts all its probability on a, so that each sample of it is a. It is written as a density that is zero away from a and integrates to 1, although it has no density in the ordinary sense, and it acts on a continuous function f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} by the sifting property \int \delta(x - y)\, f(y)\, dy = f(x).

The marginal probability path p_t is the distribution of a point sampled from the conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) with x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}},

\boxed{x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, \quad x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x \sim p_t} \tag{10}

so its density is the mixture

\boxed{p_t(x) = \int p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1} \tag{11}

The integral over the data makes this density intractable, but Eq. 10 samples from p_t without it.

The marginal path p_t runs from the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} to the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}},

\boxed{p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}, \qquad p_1 = p_{\mathrm{data}}} \tag{12}

NoteProof: the endpoints of the marginal path

Setting t = 0 in Eq. 11,

p_0(x) = \int p_0(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the boundary condition p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}} of Eq. 9,

p_0(x) = \int p_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking p_{\mathrm{init}}(x), which does not depend on x_1, out of the integral,

p_0(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}(x) \int p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Since p_{\mathrm{data}} integrates to 1,

p_0(x) = p_{\mathrm{init}}(x)

Setting t = 1 in Eq. 11,

p_1(x) = \int p_1(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the boundary condition p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \delta(\cdot - x_1) of Eq. 9,

p_1(x) = \int \delta(x - x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

By the sifting property of the Dirac delta,

p_1(x) = p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)

Together with the value at t = 0, this is Eq. 12. \square

4.1.1 Gaussian conditional path to a spiral

A two-dimensional example after Holderrieth and Erives [10] shows the two paths, with a Gaussian p_{\mathrm{init}} and a p_{\mathrm{data}} shaped into a spiral by a Lamb-Oseen vortex.

Initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}: The standard Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I) on \mathbb{R}^2.

Data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}: A spiral built from a disk using a Lamb-Oseen vortex, as Figure 5 and Figure 6 show below. The disk has radius \rho = 1.2 and center c = (1.5, 0) (left panel of Figure 5). Each of its points is carried by the flow \phi_1 of the Lamb-Oseen vortex of §3.1.1, with \kappa = 40.5 and r_c = 1.2, which turns a point at distance r from the origin by the angle \omega(r).

The angle \omega(r) is largest near the origin and falls off with distance, so the side of the disk nearest the origin winds into the inner turns of the spiral and the far side forms its outer end (right panel).

Figure 6 below animates the construction, turning each point of the disk by the fraction s of its angle \omega(r) as s runs from 0 to 1.

The resulting p_{\mathrm{data}} is uniform on the spiral. With D the disk of radius \rho centered at c, and p_{\mathrm{data}}(r, \vartheta) its density at the point with polar coordinates (r, \vartheta),

p_{\mathrm{data}}(r, \vartheta) = \begin{cases} 1 / (\pi \rho^2), & (r,\ \vartheta - \omega(r)) \in D \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

The spiral is the set of points that turning back by \omega(r), (r, \vartheta) \mapsto (r, \vartheta - \omega(r)), sends into D. That turn preserves the area element r\, dr\, d\vartheta, so the spiral has the area \pi \rho^2 of D and p_{\mathrm{data}} integrates to 1.

Conditional path: The example uses a conditional probability path of Lipman et al. that is Gaussian at each time [7],

p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}\big(t\, x_1,\ (1 - t)^2 I\big)

At t = 0 it is \mathcal{N}(0, I) = p_{\mathrm{init}}. At t = 1 its variance is zero, and a Gaussian with zero variance is the Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - x_1), so both boundary conditions of Eq. 9 hold. A sample of it is t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). The path contracts the Gaussian onto x_1, as its mean t\, x_1 runs along the segment from the origin to x_1 and its standard deviation 1 - t falls from one to zero. The left animation of Figure 7 below shows this path for one fixed x_1, marked by the star, and the right animation the marginal path p_t.

Marginal path: By Eq. 10, sampling x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and then t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, \epsilon gives a sample of the marginal path p_t, so p_t is the distribution of t\, x_1, the spiral contracted toward the origin by the factor t, convolved with \mathcal{N}(0, (1 - t)^2 I). The right animation shows it. At t = 0 it starts at the same Gaussian as the conditional path does, but at t = 1, instead of at a single point x_1, it ends at p_{\mathrm{data}}, the spiral.

4.2 Conditional and marginal velocity fields

A probability path prescribes the distribution that the solution X_t of an ODE should have at each time. This section defines the velocity fields of such ODEs, first for the conditional probability path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) of each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d (§4.2.1) and then, by averaging these fields over x_1, for the marginal probability path p_t (§4.2.2). §4.5 proves that the solution of the averaged field’s ODE has p_t as its distribution at each time. Lipman et al. [7] and Holderrieth and Erives [10] call the two fields defined below the conditional and marginal vector fields.

4.2.1 Conditional velocity field

For each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, a conditional velocity field u(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto u_t(x \mid x_1), is a velocity field whose ODE solution, with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and with X_1 = \lim_{t \to 1} X_t, has the conditional probability path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) of §4.1 as its distribution at each time t,

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = u_t(X_t \mid x_1) \ \ (t < 1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) \quad \forall t \in [0, 1]} \tag{13}

By Eq. 13 and the endpoint \delta(\cdot - x_1) of Eq. 9, the ODE solution of the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) ends at X_1 = x_1. In isolation, the conditional velocity field is of little use, as it carries a distribution to a single point, but taking a weighted average of these conditional fields over x_1 gives a marginal velocity field that carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}}.

4.2.2 Marginal velocity field

Averaging the conditional velocity fields over x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, weighted by how likely each x_1 is to have produced the point x, gives the marginal velocity field u: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto u_t(x),

\boxed{u_t(x) = \int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, \frac{p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}{p_t(x)}\, dx_1 \qquad p_t(x) > 0} \tag{14}

By Bayes’ rule [63], the weight in Eq. 14 is the posterior p_t(\cdot \mid x): \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), x_1 \mapsto p_t(x_1 \mid x),

\frac{p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}{p_t(x)} = p_t(x_1 \mid x)

Substituting it into Eq. 14,

u_t(x) = \int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x_1 \mid x)\, dx_1

The integral is the expectation over the posterior,

\boxed{u_t(x) = \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[\, u_t(x \mid x_1) \,\big]} \tag{15}

\square

4.2.2.1 The marginal velocity as a posterior average

For the spiral example of §4.1.1, the conditional path \mathcal{N}\big(t\, x_1, (1 - t)^2 I\big) is the distribution of X_t = t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, X_0 with X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}. This X_t satisfies \frac{d}{dt} X_t = x_1 - X_0 = (x_1 - X_t)/(1 - t), so u_t(x \mid x_1) = (x_1 - x)/(1 - t) is a conditional velocity field of the path, since the ODE has a unique solution (§3.1).

By Eq. 15, the marginal velocity field at a point x is the average of these fields under the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x), which is proportional to \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ t\, x_1, (1 - t)^2 I\big)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1). As a function of x_1, the Gaussian factor is proportional to \mathcal{N}\big(x_1;\ x / t,\ ((1 - t)/t)^2 I\big), so the posterior is p_{\mathrm{data}} reweighted by a Gaussian centered at x / t with standard deviation (1 - t)/t. The average at one point x and two times is drawn as arrows, as Figure 8 shows below.

At t = 0.25 the standard deviation is 3, wider than the spiral, so the posterior spreads over the whole spiral and the conditional velocities point in all directions. They largely cancel in the average, and the thick arrow ends at the posterior mean (0.72, -0.27), between the arms, where p_{\mathrm{data}} has no mass.

At t = 0.8 the standard deviation is 0.25, so the posterior concentrates on the part of the arm just outside x near x / t = (1.25, -1), and the average follows the few arrows that carry its weight. As (1 - t)/t falls from infinity to zero, u_t at each point averages over the whole spiral early and over the nearby data late.

4.3 The continuity equation

The continuity equation, first written by Euler for the density of a fluid [4], is a partial differential equation that relates a probability path p_t to a velocity field v_t(x),

\boxed{\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big( p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \big) = 0} \tag{16}

The product p_t(x)\, v_t(x) is the probability flux, the probability mass that crosses a unit area per unit time. In a time \Delta t, the probability that crosses a unit area perpendicular to v_t(x) is the mass of the particles within the length \lVert v_t(x) \rVert\, \Delta t behind it, p_t(x)\, \lVert v_t(x) \rVert\, \Delta t, so per unit time the flux is p_t(x)\, \lVert v_t(x) \rVert, along v_t(x). Figure 9 below shows this flux (left) and its net outflow from a small box (right).

Here \nabla_x \cdot is the divergence, defined in §3.4. The divergence of the flux is its net outflow per unit volume, as the right panel shows. For a box of width h, the flux out through its faces minus the flux in, divided by its volume, tends to \nabla_x \cdot \big(p_t(x)\, v_t(x)\big) as h \to 0. So Eq. 16 states that the density at a point changes only by the net outflow of the flux, which is conservation of probability.

The continuity equation is the deterministic special case of the d-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation, P1:Eq. 45, which for an SDE dx = f(x, t)\,dt + g(t)\,dW, with drift f, diffusion coefficient g and W a Brownian motion, is

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x \cdot (f\, p_t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

where \Delta_x = \nabla_x \cdot \nabla_x is the Laplacian. Setting g \equiv 0 and f(x, t) = v_t(x) turns the SDE into the ODE of v_t(x) and the Fokker-Planck equation into Eq. 16.

Along each trajectory, the continuity equation gives the rate of change of the log-density of §3.4 without Jacobi’s formula. Let v_t(x) be continuously differentiable in x and Lipschitz, as in §3.4, let p_t be positive, continuously differentiable in (t, x) and satisfy Eq. 16, and let \phi_t be the flow of v_t (Eq. 5). By the chain rule,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{(\partial_t p_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big) + \frac{d}{dt}\phi_t(x) \cdot (\nabla_x p_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)}{p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big)}

Substituting \frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x) = v_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) from Eq. 5,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{\partial_t p_t + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Substituting \partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) from Eq. 16,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-\nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Expanding the divergence of the product, \nabla_x \cdot (p_t\, v_t) = v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t + p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t - p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t + v_t \cdot \nabla_x p_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Cancelling the two terms with \nabla_x p_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = \frac{-p_t\, \nabla_x \cdot v_t}{p_t}\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

Cancelling the factor p_t, which is positive,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \log p_t\big(\phi_t(x)\big) = -(\nabla_x \cdot v_t)\big(\phi_t(x)\big)

which is the rate that §3.4 derived from the Jacobian of the flow, and integrating it gives Eq. 7.

4.4 Distribution of an ODE’s solution ⟺ continuity equation

This section states and proves the equivalence between the continuity equation Eq. 16 and the distribution of the solution of an ODE, on a time interval (0, T] with T > 0. Its proofs adapt those of the Fokker-Planck equivalence in P3:§2.1 to an equation with no diffusion term.

That equivalence, with zero diffusion, already covers an ODE whose velocity field is infinitely differentiable with bounded derivatives and whose initial condition is at t = 0. The theorem below needs only a continuously differentiable Lipschitz velocity field and allows the initial condition at a time t_0 \in (0, T], with the ODE solved in both directions. Part 5 needs this generality, since generation there solves the probability-flow ODE backward from t_0 = T.

In the theorem, the velocity field and the probability path are defined for t \in (0, T] instead of [0, 1], the interval of §3.1 and §3.2.1.

Definitions:

  • A velocity field v_t(x) satisfies the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions when it is Lipschitz in x uniformly in t with a constant K, as defined in §3.1 with (0, T] in place of [0, 1], and \lVert v_t(x) \rVert \le K\, (1 + \lVert x \rVert) for each x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in (0, T].
  • A function of x decays at infinity when it and its first two derivatives tend to zero as \lVert x \rVert \to \infty fast enough to leave no boundary terms when it is integrated by parts against a bounded function with bounded derivatives. This must hold also after the function is multiplied by one that grows at most linearly in x, such as a velocity field that satisfies the linear-growth condition.
