  • A probability path p_t is dominated when, on each interval [a, b] with 0 < a \le b \le T, the functions (1 + \lVert x \rVert)\, p_t(x) and \lvert \partial_t p_t(x) \rvert, for t \in [a, b], are bounded by one integrable function of x.

Assumptions:

  1. The velocity field v_t(x) is continuously differentiable and satisfies the Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions. So exactly one trajectory passes through each point at each time.
  2. The ODE \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = v_t(X_t) has the initial condition X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in (0, T] and is solved forward and backward in time from there. Its solution is X_t.
  3. The probability path p_t is continuously differentiable in t and twice continuously differentiable in x, decays at infinity for each t and is dominated.

Theorem:

Under these assumptions,

\boxed{\begin{aligned} &X_t \sim p_t \ \forall t \in (0, T] \\[4pt] \Longleftrightarrow\quad &\partial_t p_t(x) + \nabla_x \cdot \big( p_t(x)\, v_t(x) \big) = 0 \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ t \in (0, T] \end{aligned}} \tag{17}

The left side of Eq. 17 states that p_t is the distribution of X_t at each time, and the right side is the continuity equation Eq. 16. So the continuity equation is a necessary and sufficient condition for p_t to be the distribution of X_t.

  • Necessity (\Rightarrow): If the solution X_t of the ODE of v_t(x) has X_t \sim p_t for each t, then p_t and v_t(x) satisfy Eq. 16.
  • Sufficiency (\Leftarrow): If p_t and v_t(x) satisfy Eq. 16, then the solution X_t of the ODE of v_t(x) with the initial condition X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} has X_t \sim p_t for each t.

4.4.1 Proof of necessity (⇒)

The ODE is the SDE with drift v_t and diffusion coefficient g = 0. The derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation in P1:§8.3 applies Itô’s lemma to a test function, a function \psi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} that is infinitely differentiable and zero outside a bounded set, and integrates by parts. It holds for g = 0, where Itô’s lemma reduces to the chain rule, with the time integrals taken from t_0 instead of 0, which the chain rule allows in either direction of time.

The derivation’s hypotheses hold here, since assumption 3 makes p_t continuously differentiable in t and twice in x, and assumptions 1 and 3 make v_t continuous and v_t\, p_t continuously differentiable in x. So p_t, the distribution of X_t by the left side of Eq. 17, satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation with the drift v_t and with g = 0,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 \cdot \Delta_x p_t

Dropping the zero diffusion term,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big)

Moving the divergence to the left-hand side,

\boxed{\partial_t p_t + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big) = 0}

which is Eq. 16. \square

4.4.2 Proof of sufficiency (⇐)

The proof is the argument of P3:§2.1.2, which proves the sufficiency part of the Fokker-Planck equivalence, with g = 0 and the initial condition at t_0. It is outlined here and given in full below. The solution of the ODE is deterministic, which changes the first two steps.

  1. The function U(x, t) = \psi(Y_s), the value of a test function \psi at time s along the trajectory Y through x at time t, carries the test function along the trajectories.
  2. U is constant along each trajectory, so by the chain rule it satisfies the transport equation \partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U = 0, the backward Kolmogorov equation with g = 0.
  3. When p_t satisfies the continuity equation, \int U\, p_t\, dx is constant in time, as in post #3.
  4. Comparing its values at t = t_0, where X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0}, and at t = s gives \int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}[\psi(X_s)] for each test function, so p_s is the density of X_s.
NoteProof: sufficiency of the continuity equation

Let p_t satisfy the continuity equation, and fix s \in (0, T] and a test function \psi.

Step 1 — a function that carries the test function along the trajectories:

Let \mathcal{T} be the closed interval between s and t_0. For x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in \mathcal{T}, let Y: \mathcal{T} \to \mathbb{R}^d, r \mapsto Y_r, be the trajectory with Y_t = x. With g = 0, the function of post #3’s proof becomes U: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal{T} \to \mathbb{R},

U(x, t) = \psi(Y_s)

the value of \psi at time s along the trajectory through x at time t. At t = s, Y_s = x, so U(x, s) = \psi(x).

Step 3 needs U to be bounded with a bounded gradient. It is bounded because \psi is. Under assumption 1, the trajectory depends continuously differentiably on x and t [48], [58], so U is continuously differentiable, and its gradient is bounded once nearby trajectories separate at a bounded rate.

For two trajectories Y and Y', the rate of change of \chi: \mathcal{T} \to [0, \infty), r \mapsto \lVert Y_r - Y'_r \rVert^2, is 2\,(Y_r - Y'_r) \cdot \big(v_r(Y_r) - v_r(Y'_r)\big), at most 2K\chi(r) in absolute value, where K is the Lipschitz constant of v_t. Grönwall’s inequality [58], that \lvert \chi' \rvert \le 2K\chi implies \chi(s) \le \chi(t)\, e^{2K\lvert s - t \rvert}, then shows that the trajectories Y, Y' through two points x, y at time t are at most \lVert x - y \rVert\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert} apart at time s.

So, with C the Lipschitz constant of the test function \psi, \lvert U(x, t) - U(y, t) \rvert = \lvert \psi(Y_s) - \psi(Y'_s) \rvert \le C\, \lVert x - y \rVert\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert}. The gradient of U is therefore bounded by C\, e^{K\lvert t - s \rvert}.

Step 2 — U satisfies the transport equation:

Let x \in \mathbb{R}^d and t \in \mathcal{T} be fixed, with Y the trajectory of Step 1. For each r \in \mathcal{T}, the trajectory through Y_r at time r is Y itself, because exactly one trajectory passes through each point at each time (assumption 1). By the definition of U,

U(Y_r, r) = \psi(Y_s)

Differentiating both sides in r, the left by the chain rule with dY_r/dr = v_r(Y_r) and the right, which does not depend on r, to zero,

\partial_t U(Y_r, r) + v_r(Y_r)\cdot\nabla_x U(Y_r, r) = 0

Setting r = t, where Y_t = x,

\partial_t U(x, t) + v_t(x)\cdot\nabla_x U(x, t) = 0

This holds for each x and each t \in \mathcal{T}. Together with U(x, s) = \psi(x) from Step 1, U satisfies the transport equation, the backward Kolmogorov equation of post #3’s proof with g = 0,

\partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U = 0, \qquad U(x, s) = \psi(x)

Step 3 — the integral of U against p_t is constant on \mathcal{T}:

Differentiating \int U\, p_t\, dx in t under the integral, for t in the interior of \mathcal{T}, which the domination of assumption 3 permits because U is bounded and \partial_t U = -v_t\cdot\nabla_x U grows at most linearly in x (Steps 1 and 2, assumption 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx + \int U\, \partial_t p_t\, dx

Substituting the continuity equation for \partial_t p_t,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx - \int U\, \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, v_t\big)\, dx

Integrating the second term by parts, with no boundary term because p_t decays at infinity (assumption 3), v_t grows at most linearly (assumption 1) and U is bounded with a bounded gradient (Step 1),

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \partial_t U\, p_t\, dx + \int v_t\cdot\nabla_x U\; p_t\, dx

Combining the two integrals,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = \int \big(\partial_t U + v_t\cdot\nabla_x U\big)\, p_t\, dx

Substituting the transport equation of Step 2,

\frac{d}{dt}\int U\, p_t\, dx = 0

This holds for each t in the interior of \mathcal{T}, and \int U\, p_t\, dx is continuous on \mathcal{T} by the same domination, so it is constant on \mathcal{T}.

Step 4 — \int \psi\, p_s\, dx equals \mathbb{E}[\psi(X_s)]:

Using U(x, s) = \psi(x) from Step 1,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \int U(x, s)\, p_s(x)\, dx

By Step 3, the integral takes the same value at t = t_0,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \int U(x, t_0)\, p_{t_0}(x)\, dx

Since X_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} (assumption 2),

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[U(X_{t_0}, t_0)\big]

Substituting U(X_{t_0}, t_0) = \psi(X_s), since X_s lies on the trajectory through X_{t_0} at time t_0,

\int \psi\, p_s\, dx = \mathbb{E}\big[\psi(X_s)\big]

A density that gives each test function its expected value under X_s is the density of X_s, so X_s \sim p_s. As s \in (0, T] was arbitrary, X_t \sim p_t for each t \in (0, T]. \square

4.5 Marginal velocity field ⟹ marginal path

This section applies Eq. 17 to the conditional and the marginal velocity fields.

Assumptions:

  1. On each interval [0, T] with T < 1, each conditional pair \big(p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), u_t(\cdot \mid x_1)\big) and the marginal pair (p_t, u_t) meet assumptions 1 and 3 of §4.4, with the domination of assumption 3 holding on each interval [a, b] with 0 \le a \le b \le T. §4.4 places the initial condition at a time t_0 \in (0, T], and its proofs use only the interval between t_0 and the time considered, so Eq. 17 holds here with the initial condition at t_0 = 0.
  2. For t \in [0, 1), the functions \partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1) and the first x-derivatives of u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1) are bounded, locally uniformly in (x, t), by a p_{\mathrm{data}}-integrable function of x_1.
  3. The conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) converges in distribution to \delta(\cdot - x_1) as t \to 1.
  4. The solution of the ODE of u_t with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} exists on [0, 1].

Assumption 1 lets Eq. 17 apply to the conditional and the marginal pairs, and assumption 2 lets derivatives pass under the integral over x_1. Both stop short of t = 1, where the conditional path is the Dirac delta \delta(\cdot - x_1), which has no derivatives in the ordinary sense, and a conditional velocity field can grow without bound. For the Gaussian path of §4.1.1, the conditional velocity field u_t(x \mid x_1) = (x_1 - x)/(1 - t) of §4.2.2.1 is unbounded near t = 1 at each x \neq x_1. Assumptions 3 and 4 handle t = 1.

Theorem:

Under these assumptions, the ODE solution of the marginal velocity field u_t, with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, has the marginal probability path p_t as its distribution at each time t \in [0, 1],

\boxed{X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, \quad \frac{d}{dt}\, X_t = u_t(X_t) \ \ (t < 1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_t \sim p_t \quad \forall t \in [0, 1]} \tag{18}

In particular X_1 \sim p_1 = p_{\mathrm{data}} by Eq. 12, so u_t carries the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} to the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}}.

The theorem is the flow counterpart of Gyöngy’s mimicking theorem for Itô processes [37], in which a diffusion whose drift and diffusion matrix are the conditional expectations, given the current state, of another Itô process’s drift and diffusion matrix has the same distribution at each time. Brigo stated the mixture form for diffusions [65] and Peluchetti in general [66], and Lipman et al. note that their Theorem 1, the statement above for flows, also follows from Peluchetti’s result [7].

Proof:

For t \in [0, 1), Eq. 13 states that the solution of the ODE of u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) has X_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1). So by the necessity part of Eq. 17, which applies by assumption 1, each conditional pair satisfies Eq. 16,

\partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]

Integrating both sides against p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1),

\int \partial_t p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking \partial_t outside the integral on the left, which assumption 2 allows,

\partial_t \int p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Substituting the marginal path Eq. 11,

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\int \nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1

Taking \nabla_x\cdot outside the integral, which assumption 2 also allows,

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \Big[\int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1\Big]

By Eq. 14, the bracketed integral is u_t(x)\, p_t(x),

\partial_t p_t(x) = -\nabla_x \!\cdot\! \big[u_t(x)\, p_t(x)\big]

So the marginal pair (p_t, u_t) satisfies Eq. 16 on (0, 1), and the marginal path starts at p_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}} by Eq. 12. By the sufficiency part of Eq. 17 on (0, T] for each T < 1, with the initial condition at t_0 = 0, which applies by assumption 1, the solution of the ODE of u_t with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} has X_t \sim p_t for each t \in [0, 1).

As t \to 1, X_t \to X_1 along each trajectory, because the solution exists on [0, 1] (assumption 4). Each conditional path converges in distribution to \delta(\cdot - x_1) (assumption 3), so by dominated convergence over x_1 their mixture p_t converges in distribution to \int \delta(\cdot - x_1)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1 = p_1. A limit in distribution is unique, so X_1 \sim p_1 as well, which is Eq. 18. \square

4.5.1 Generated paths and the non-uniqueness of the velocity field

A velocity field v_t(x) generates a probability path p_t when the two satisfy Eq. 16, so the proof above shows that the marginal velocity field u_t generates the marginal path p_t on (0, 1).

The continuity equation does not determine the velocity field that generates a probability path. A field w: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1) \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto w_t(x), is divergence-free when \nabla_x \cdot w_t = 0 for each t. For a divergence-free w, adding w_t / p_t to u_t adds w_t to the flux p_t\, u_t without changing its divergence, so u_t + w_t / p_t also generates p_t. Eq. 14 is one choice among these, the one the flow-matching loss of §5.2 regresses onto.

5 Flow Matching

This Part carries out the third step. It begins with the probability-flow ODE of diffusion, the first flow model trained without solving its ODE, whose fixed path motivated flow matching, and derives it a second way, through the continuity equation (§5.1). It then defines the flow-matching objective, which is intractable, and proves that the conditional flow matching objective has the same gradient (§5.2). It ends with conditioning on any latent variable, the training algorithm and sampling. Part 6 makes the procedure concrete for Gaussian conditional paths.

5.1 The probability-flow ODE: training without solving the ODE

Song et al. gave the first flow model trained without solving its ODE [12]. Its velocity field is built from a diffusion model’s score, which DSM learns by regression (P3:§4), so training never solves the ODE.

The solution of the probability-flow ODE of post #3 has the diffusion marginals, which post #3 proves through the Fokker-Planck equation and §5.1.1 below proves a second way, through the continuity equation of §4.4.

Here f(x,t) and g(t) are the drift and diffusion coefficients of the forward SDE dx = f\,dt + g\,dW (P3:Eq. 1). The field below is stated in the diffusion’s own time, where t = 0 is data and t increases toward noise up to the terminal time T, the reverse of this post’s convention. In this section p_t likewise denotes the diffusion marginals, which start at p_0 = p_{\mathrm{data}}. From §5.2 on, t is again the time of this post’s convention and p_t the marginal path of Part 4.

The probability-flow ODE is dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t), with the velocity field \tilde f: \mathbb{R}^d \times (0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^d,

\boxed{\tilde f(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x)} \tag{19}

As written it transports data to noise.

The path, however, is fixed by the forward SDE, and three pitfalls follow, the first two pointed out by Lipman et al. [7] and Liu et al. [8]. The marginals reach the noise distribution only as the diffusion time goes to infinity, so the initial distribution of generation is an approximation (§6.2). The VP trajectories are curved and move slowly at first (§6.4). And the velocity is available only through the score, whose regression target, the conditional score, diverges where the noise vanishes (P3:§4.2.3). Flow matching keeps the regression and frees the path.

5.1.1 Deriving the probability-flow ODE using the continuity equation

The derivation, for data supported in a bounded set, has three steps. Step 1 shows that the diffusion marginals p_t satisfy a continuity equation, with the velocity field \tilde f of Eq. 19. Step 2 checks that v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t) and p_t meet the assumptions of the equivalence of §4.4. Step 3 combines the two. By the sufficiency part of that equivalence, p_t is the distribution of the solution of the ODE with the velocity field \tilde f, the probability-flow ODE. P3:§A.4 treats the general SDE.

Step 1 — p_t satisfies a continuity equation:

Starting from the Fokker-Planck equation of the forward SDE, which p_t satisfies by the necessity part of P3:Eq. 18,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \Delta_x p_t

Substituting the log-derivative identity \Delta_x p_t = \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big) of P3:Eq. 19, which follows from \nabla_x \log p_t = \nabla_x p_t / p_t,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\big)

Writing \tfrac{1}{2} g^2, which depends on t only, inside the divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(f\, p_t\big) + \nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, p_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)

Combining into one divergence,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\Big[\Big(f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t\Big)\, p_t\Big]

Substituting the velocity field \tilde f = f - \tfrac{1}{2} g^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t of Eq. 19,

\partial_t p_t = -\nabla_x\!\cdot\!\big(\tilde f\, p_t\big) \tag{20}

So the diffusion marginals p_t, which satisfy the Fokker-Planck equation, also satisfy the continuity equation with the velocity field \tilde f.

Step 2 — the assumptions of the equivalence hold:

The equivalence of §4.4 has three assumptions, and each holds for v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t) and p_t on each interval [t_{\min}, T] with t_{\min} > 0, in place of (0, T].

Assumption 1 — Lipschitz velocity field: The drift f is affine in x for each SDE of post #3, so it is Lipschitz. For data supported in a solid sphere of radius R centered at the origin, P3:Eq. 21 bounds each derivative of \log p_t of order two or more uniformly in time, \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\, t \in [t_{\min}, T]} \lVert \nabla_x^k \log p_t(x) \rVert < \infty for each k \ge 2, where \nabla_x^k is the k-th derivative in x. With order two it bounds the Hessian of \log p_t, so the score \nabla_x \log p_t is Lipschitz in x. Both terms of \tilde f are continuously differentiable and Lipschitz, so \tilde f is too, and hence of at most linear growth.

Assumption 2 — initial condition: The ODE dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t) has the initial condition x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in [t_{\min}, T], and x_t denotes its solution. Solving forward from a t_0 near 0 maps data to noise, and solving backward from t_0 = T generates samples.

Assumption 3 — regularity and decay at infinity: The marginal p_t is a Gaussian convolution of data with bounded support, so it is smooth in t and x, decays at infinity and is dominated, because its Gaussian tails, and those of \partial_t p_t, are uniform in t on each [a, b] \subset (0, T].

Step 3 — the sufficiency part applies:

By Step 1, p_t satisfies the continuity equation Eq. 20 with v_t = \tilde f(\cdot, t), and by Step 2 the assumptions of Eq. 17 hold. Its sufficiency part therefore makes p_t the distribution of x_t for each t \in [t_{\min}, T], where x_t is the solution of the ODE dx_t/dt = \tilde f(x_t, t) with the initial condition x_{t_0} \sim p_{t_0} at a time t_0 \in [t_{\min}, T]. As t_{\min} > 0 is arbitrary, this holds for each t_0 \in (0, T] and each t \in (0, T]. Writing \tilde f out, the ODE is

\boxed{\frac{dx_t}{dt} = f(x_t, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}\, g(t)^2\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)}

which is the probability-flow ODE with the velocity field Eq. 19. \square

5.2 Flow-matching loss

The network is trained to equal the marginal velocity field u_t, since its trajectories then follow the marginal path p_t by Eq. 18.

5.2.1 The objective we wish we could optimize

The natural objective regresses the network onto the marginal velocity field u_t of Eq. 14,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t} \big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \|^2 \,\big]} \tag{21}

This objective is simulation-free, which means that training with it never solves the ODE, unlike maximum-likelihood training of a flow model [3]. The obstacle is that the density p_t is intractable, and with it u_t, which divides by it.

5.2.2 Conditional flow matching

The conditional flow matching objective regresses the network onto the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1), which the choice of conditional path makes known in closed form, at points sampled by Eq. 10,

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x \mid x_1)} \big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big]} \tag{22}

The central theorem of flow matching is Lipman et al.’s Theorem 2 [7].

Assumptions:

  1. The marginal path is positive, p_t(x) > 0 for each x \in \mathbb{R}^d and each t \in [0, 1), so that the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x) of §4.2.2 is defined.
  2. Under t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1], x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} and x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), the second moments \mathbb{E}\lVert v_\theta(x, t) \rVert^2, for each \theta, and \mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2 are finite, which makes both objectives and each term of their expanded squares finite.

Theorem:

Under these assumptions, the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 22 and the objective Eq. 21 differ by a constant that does not depend on \theta, so they have the same gradient,

\boxed{\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)} \tag{23}

Minimizing the tractable conditional flow matching objective Eq. 22 therefore trains v_\theta(x, t) to match the intractable marginal velocity field u_t.

This equivalence is the flow-matching analogue of Vincent’s equivalence between explicit and denoising score matching [67], which P2:§4.8 proves.

Proof:

The identity Eq. 15, derived in §4.2.2, gives the gradient equality.

By the definition Eq. 22,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big]

Expanding the square, into three expectations that are finite by assumption 2, the cross term because \lvert a \cdot b \rvert \le \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert a \rVert^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert b \rVert^2,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|u_t(x \mid x_1)\|^2\big]

The last term carries no \theta; naming it C_1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + C_1

Averaging over x_1 then x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) reproduces the marginal p_t; for the first term, whose integrand has no x_1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big] + C_1

Writing the joint density of (x_1, x) in the cross term as p_t(x)\, p_t(x_1 \mid x), by Bayes’ rule (§4.2.2) with the posterior defined by assumption 1,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\Big] + C_1

Taking v_\theta(x, t), which does not depend on x_1, out of the inner expectation,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\Big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\big[u_t(x \mid x_1)\big]\Big] + C_1

Substituting the identity Eq. 15,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x)\big] + C_1

Adding and subtracting C_2 = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|u_t(x)\|^2\big], which is free of \theta and finite, since Eq. 15 gives \lVert u_t(x) \rVert^2 \le \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2 (their difference is the conditional variance \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}\lVert u_t(x \mid x_1) - u_t(x) \rVert^2 \ge 0), so that averaging over x \sim p_t and t gives C_2 \le C_1, which is finite by assumption 2,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\|v_\theta(x, t)\|^2\big] - 2\, \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[v_\theta(x, t) \cdot u_t(x)\big] + C_2 + (C_1 - C_2)

Completing the square,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_t}\big[\, \| v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x) \|^2 \,\big] + (C_1 - C_2)

By the definition Eq. 21,

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) + (C_1 - C_2)

The two objectives therefore differ only by the \theta-independent constant C_1 - C_2, so they have the same minimizers, and if the family \{v_\theta\} contains u_t, the minimizer satisfies v_\theta(x, t) = u_t(x) for p_t-almost every x, at almost every t. Taking the gradient in \theta, which annihilates the constant,

\boxed{\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)}

which is Eq. 23. \square

5.2.2.1 General conditioning

Neither the proof of Eq. 18 in §4.5 nor the proof above uses that the conditioning variable is x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. The conditioning variable can be any latent variable z \sim q, with q a distribution on \mathbb{R}^k, conditional paths p_t(x \mid z) and conditional velocity fields u_t(x \mid z). Both proofs then carry over when the conditional paths have densities. Integrals against q replace those against p_{\mathrm{data}}, the marginal velocity field u_t is defined by Eq. 14 with z and q in place of x_1 and p_{\mathrm{data}}, and the tower property of conditional expectation, that the expectation of a conditional expectation is the unconditional expectation, applies as before.

The boundary conditions do not carry over, since p_0(\cdot \mid z) need no longer equal the initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}}. What must be checked instead is that the mixtures satisfy \int p_0(x \mid z)\, q(z)\, dz = p_{\mathrm{init}} and \int p_1(x \mid z)\, q(z)\, dz = p_{\mathrm{data}}. Post #5 uses this with z = (x_0, x_1) sampled from a coupling, a joint distribution \gamma(x_0, x_1) whose marginals are p_{\mathrm{init}} and p_{\mathrm{data}}, so q is the coupling \gamma, with k = 2d. The conditional paths there are Dirac deltas, which have no densities, and post #5 extends the gradient equality to them.

5.2.2.2 Training and sampling

By Eq. 23, flow-matching training minimizes the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 22. It needs samples x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1] and x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), and the conditional velocity field u_t(\cdot \mid x_1) in closed form, and it never solves the ODE.

Algorithm 8 — Flow-matching training [7]:

1: repeat
    2: x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1], x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1)
    3: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \lVert v_\theta(x, t) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \rVert^2
    4: take a gradient step on \mathcal{L}(\theta)
5: until converged

In practice line 2 samples a minibatch and line 3 averages the loss over it.

If the network equals the marginal velocity field u_t, its trajectories follow the marginal path p_t by Eq. 18, so solving Eq. 6 with the initial condition X_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} ends at X_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. A trained network approximates u_t, so its X_1 approximately follows p_{\mathrm{data}}. Training by Algorithm 8 followed by sampling with Algorithm 7 is the flow-matching pipeline. §6 makes the procedure concrete for Gaussian conditional paths.

6 Gaussian Conditional Paths

This Part develops the conditional paths that Lipman et al. train on, which are Gaussian at each time [7]. It derives their conditional velocity fields and the objective they give (§6.1). It then obtains two instances, the paths of the diffusion SDEs of posts #1 and #3 (§6.2) and the path whose mean and standard deviation change linearly in time (§6.3). It compares the two on their trajectories and in Lipman et al.’s experiments (§6.4), and it ends with three pitfalls that these paths keep (§6.5).

6.1 Gaussian paths and their conditional velocity fields

Lipman et al. train on conditional paths that are Gaussian at each time, which meet the two needs of the conditional flow matching objective Eq. 22. They can be sampled, and their conditional velocity fields are known in closed form. A Gaussian conditional path has, for each x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d, the form

\boxed{p_t(x \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}\big(x;\ m_t(x_1),\ \sigma_t(x_1)^2\, I\big)} \tag{24}

with a mean m: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d, (t, x_1) \mapsto m_t(x_1), and a standard deviation \sigma: [0, 1] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to [0, \infty), (t, x_1) \mapsto \sigma_t(x_1), both differentiable in t. With p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I), the boundary conditions Eq. 9 fix their values at the two ends,

m_0(x_1) = 0, \quad \sigma_0(x_1) = 1, \qquad m_1(x_1) = x_1, \quad \sigma_1(x_1) = 0

Between the two ends we require \sigma_t(x_1) > 0 for t \in [0, 1), so that p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) has a density before t = 1. Lipman et al. end the path at a small \sigma_1(x_1) = \sigma_{\min} > 0, a narrow Gaussian around x_1, in place of the Dirac delta of Eq. 9. This post uses \sigma_{\min} = 0, which keeps the Dirac delta. Below, m_t and \sigma_t stand for m_t(x_1) and \sigma_t(x_1) at a fixed x_1.

Each Gaussian conditional path is the pushforward of p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I) under an affine map. That map is the conditional flow \phi(\cdot \mid x_1): \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, (x, t) \mapsto \phi_t(x \mid x_1),

\boxed{\phi_t(x \mid x_1) = \sigma_t\, x + m_t} \tag{25}

It carries x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} to \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) \sim \mathcal{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2\, I) = p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), because an affine function \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t of a standard Gaussian is Gaussian with mean m_t and covariance \sigma_t^2\, I.

Many velocity fields generate the same path, as §4.5.1 shows. Lipman et al. choose the one whose flow is this affine map, the simplest of them [7]. The others add components that leave the distribution unchanged, such as rotations about m_t, which preserve the isotropic Gaussian \mathcal{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2\, I), and these components only add computation.

Differentiating the conditional flow in t at a fixed x_0, with \dot\sigma_t = d\sigma_t/dt and \dot m_t = dm_t/dt,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t

Writing x for the point \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) and substituting x_0 = (x - m_t)/\sigma_t, which inverts Eq. 25 for t \in [0, 1), where \sigma_t > 0,

\frac{d}{dt}\, \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t

By Eq. 5, the velocity field whose flow is \phi_t(\cdot \mid x_1) takes this value at x, so it is

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, (x - m_t) + \dot m_t \qquad t \in [0, 1)} \tag{26}

Its flow is the conditional flow Eq. 25, which carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_t(\cdot \mid x_1), so it is a conditional velocity field in the sense of Eq. 13 on [0, 1). This is Lipman et al.’s Theorem 3. \square

The conditional flow also simplifies training. Changing variables in Eq. 22 from x \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) to x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, with x = \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) = \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,

\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, &\| v_\theta(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,\ t) \\[4pt] &- u_t(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t \mid x_1) \|^2 \,\big] \end{aligned}

Since the conditional velocity field at \phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) is the velocity of the conditional flow, u_t\big(\phi_t(x_0 \mid x_1) \mid x_1\big) = \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t by differentiating Eq. 25 in t,

\boxed{\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, &\| v_\theta(\sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t,\ t) \\[4pt] &- (\dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t) \|^2 \,\big] \end{aligned}} \tag{27}

\square

The target \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t has no factor 1/\sigma_t, so it stays bounded up to t = 1 whenever \dot\sigma_t and \dot m_t do. Evaluating u_t(x \mid x_1) from Eq. 26 at a sampled x instead divides x - m_t by \sigma_t, which tends to 0 as t \to 1. When \dot\sigma_t itself diverges at t = 1, the target diverges too.

6.2 Diffusion conditional paths

The perturbation kernels of the diffusion SDEs of posts #1 and #3, with time reversed, have the Gaussian form Eq. 24. The time is reversed because diffusion has the data at t = 0, where flow matching has the noise. Lipman et al. set the terminal time T of the diffusion to 1, and the point the kernel conditions on, x_0 in posts #1 and #3, is written x_1 here.

The VP SDE has, in the diffusion’s time t, the perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_1,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t))\, I\big) (P1:Eq. 41), with the noise schedule \beta: [0, 1] \to (0, \infty) and the cumulative product

\bar\alpha: [0, 1] \to (0, 1], \qquad t \mapsto \exp\Big(-\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\Big)

Reversing time in the kernel, with 1 - t in place of t, gives the VP path

m_t(x_1) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)}\, x_1, \qquad \sigma_t(x_1) = \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)}

Its conditional velocity field follows from Eq. 26. Writing \beta and \bar\alpha for \beta(1 - t) and \bar\alpha(1 - t), and substituting the VP mean into Eq. 26,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \dot m_t

Substituting \dot\sigma_t / \sigma_t = -\beta \bar\alpha / \big(2 (1 - \bar\alpha)\big), the time derivative of \log \sigma_t = \tfrac{1}{2} \log\big(1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)\big), where \frac{d}{dt} \bar\alpha(1 - t) = \beta \bar\alpha,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\beta \bar\alpha}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \dot m_t

Substituting \dot m_t = \tfrac{1}{2} \beta \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1, the time derivative of \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)}\, x_1,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\beta \bar\alpha}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}\, \big(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1\big) + \tfrac{1}{2} \beta \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1

Combining over the common denominator 2 (1 - \bar\alpha),

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{\beta\, \big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x\big)}{2 (1 - \bar\alpha)}}

\square

The VE SDE (P3:§1.3) has the perturbation kernel \mathcal{N}\big(x_1,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2\, I\big), with a noise level \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}: [0, 1] \to [0, \infty) that increases from \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(0) = 0 to \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1) \gg 1. The kernel’s variance \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2 is that of the VE kernel of post #3. Post #3’s noise level starts at a small positive value at t = 0, and \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(t)^2 is the increase of its square since then. Reversing time in the kernel gives the VE path m_t(x_1) = x_1, \sigma_t(x_1) = \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t). Substituting its derivatives \dot m_t = 0 and \dot\sigma_t = -\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t), with \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}' the derivative of \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}, into Eq. 26,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t)}{\sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)}\, (x - x_1)

Neither path meets the boundary condition p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = p_{\mathrm{init}} of Eq. 9 exactly. The VP path starts at \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha(1)}\, x_1,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(1))\, I\big), close to \mathcal{N}(0, I) only because \bar\alpha(1) is small. The VE path starts at \mathcal{N}\big(x_1,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1)^2\, I\big), close to \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1)^2\, I\big) only because \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1) is large, so for the VE path p_{\mathrm{init}} is this wider Gaussian rather than \mathcal{N}(0, I). The start of each path still depends on x_1, because a diffusion forgets its initial condition only as its time goes to infinity. The paths inherit this from the SDEs they come from [7].

On these paths the conditional velocity field is the velocity field \tilde f of the probability-flow ODE (Eq. 19) when the data distribution p_{\mathrm{data}} is the Dirac delta at x_1, written in flow time, which runs opposite to the diffusion’s time.

For the VP path, the VP SDE dx_t = -\tfrac{1}{2} \beta(t)\, x_t\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW_t (P3:Eq. 9) has the drift f(x, t) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \beta(t)\, x and the diffusion coefficient g(t) = \sqrt{\beta(t)}. Substituting these and the kernel’s score -(x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1)/(1 - \bar\alpha) into Eq. 19, and negating the result for the reversed time, gives \beta\, \big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x\big) / \big(2 (1 - \bar\alpha)\big), the field above. Post #5 shows the same for the marginal velocity field of the VP path. Lipman et al. find flow matching on these paths more stable in training than score matching on the same paths [7].

On both paths \sigma_t^2 vanishes linearly as t \to 1. For the VP path, \sigma_t^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t) \approx \beta(0)\, (1 - t). For the VE path, \sigma_t^2 = \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)^2 \approx c\, (1 - t), where c is the derivative at t = 0 of the square of post #3’s noise level. That noise level is a positive constant times an increasing exponential in t, so c > 0.

Hence \sigma_t behaves like \sqrt{1 - t} near t = 1 and \dot\sigma_t like 1/\sqrt{1 - t}, so the second moment \mathbb{E}\lVert \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t \rVert^2 of the target of Eq. 27 grows like 1/(1 - t), and its integral over [0, 1] is infinite. Lipman et al. sample t only up to 1 - 10^{-5} (their Appendix E), so that assumption 2 of §5.2.2 holds with t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1 - 10^{-5}] in place of \mathcal{U}[0, 1].

6.3 Optimal-transport conditional path

Lipman et al.’s second instance, the optimal-transport path, lets the mean and the standard deviation change linearly in time [7],

m_t(x_1) = t\, x_1, \qquad \sigma_t(x_1) = 1 - t

which is the path of §4.1.1. §6.3.1 explains its name. Lipman et al. write \sigma_t = 1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})\, t, which ends at \sigma_{\min}. The conditional flow Eq. 25 of the optimal-transport path is

\phi_t(x \mid x_1) = (1 - t)\, x + t\, x_1

Each x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} therefore moves along the segment from x_0 to x_1 at the constant velocity x_1 - x_0. Substituting the path’s derivatives, through \dot\sigma_t / \sigma_t = -1/(1 - t) and \dot m_t = x_1, into Eq. 26,

u_t(x \mid x_1) = -\frac{x - t\, x_1}{1 - t} + x_1

Combining over the common denominator 1 - t,

\boxed{u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{x_1 - x}{1 - t}} \tag{28}

which is the field that §4.2.2.1 derived from the trajectories directly. \square

6.3.1 Objective and name of the optimal-transport path

The target \dot\sigma_t\, x_0 + \dot m_t of Eq. 27 is x_1 - x_0, so the objective is

\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1)}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)} \big[\, \| v_\theta\big((1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1,\ t\big) - (x_1 - x_0) \|^2 \,\big]} \tag{29}

Lipman et al. [7] call it the optimal-transport path because, for \sigma_{\min} > 0, its conditional flow at t = 1 is the optimal-transport map [39] from p_0(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) to p_1(\cdot \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}(x_1, \sigma_{\min}^2 I). For t < 1 the flow moves each point along a straight line to its image, at constant speed. Post #5 defines optimal transport and shows why such motion is optimal.

At each point x the conditional velocity field Eq. 28 keeps the direction x_1 - x for each t, whereas that of the VP path, \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\, x_1 - \bar\alpha\, x, turns as \bar\alpha changes. The conditional flow being optimal does not make the trajectories of the marginal velocity field u_t straight, so its flow is not the motion of optimal transport from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}}, as Lipman et al. note and P5:§3.3 shows.

6.4 Diffusion and optimal-transport paths compared

Under a Gaussian conditional path, each x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} moves along the trajectory \sigma_t\, x_0 + m_t of the conditional flow. Figure 10 below draws these trajectories for the VP path and the optimal-transport path, for one x_1 and the same twelve x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}}, with markers at t = 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4.

The optimal-transport trajectories are segments traversed at constant speed, so the markers divide each into quarters. The VP trajectories are curved. Their coefficients \sqrt{\bar\alpha(1 - t)} and \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha(1 - t)} have squares that sum to one, so the pair of coefficients lies on the unit circle. Each trajectory is therefore the image of a circular arc under the linear map (a, b) \mapsto a\, x_1 + b\, x_0, an arc of an ellipse, which is curved unless x_0 and x_1 are parallel.

The first two VP markers lie near the start of each trajectory, because the coefficients change slowly while t < 1/2, so each point covers most of its trajectory after t = 1/2. Liu et al. call this a non-uniform speed, since the VP trajectories are slow at first and speed up later [8]. Lipman et al. see the same in generated images, where on the diffusion paths noise dominates until the last time steps [7]. The VE trajectories, x_1 + \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}(1 - t)\, \epsilon with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), are segments toward x_1, but their speed \lvert \sigma_{\mathrm{VE}}'(1 - t) \rvert\, \lVert \epsilon \rVert varies as well [8].

Lipman et al. trained one network with each objective and path on CIFAR-10 and on ImageNet at 32 \times 32 and 64 \times 64 pixels, and the optimal-transport path alone at 128 \times 128 [7]. The objectives are flow matching, score matching and the simple objective of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [68], a regression onto the noise. Lipman et al. report three measures.

The negative log-likelihood (NLL) in bits per dimension (§2.2) is computed with Eq. 7. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [69] is the Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to the features that a pretrained Inception network extracts from generated and from real images. The NFE (§3.5) is that of an adaptive Runge-Kutta solver [70], [71], Dormand and Prince’s [72], at tolerance 10^{-5}. Unlike Algorithm 7, which takes n equal steps, such a solver shrinks the step where the trajectory bends. Lower is better for all three, and Table 1 gives two of the datasets.

The optimal-transport path is best on each measure and needs about half the NFE of DDPM, 142 against 274 on CIFAR-10. Flow matching on the VP path already improves on score matching on the same path, so part of the gain comes from the objective and part from the path. Lipman et al. also report that the optimal-transport path lowers the FID faster during training. With fixed-step solvers on ImageNet at 32 \times 32 pixels, it reaches the same error as the diffusion models, measured against a 1000-step solution, with about 60% of their function evaluations [7].

6.5 Pitfalls

Flow matching with the optimal-transport path trains by regression and samples in fewer steps than a diffusion model, but it has three pitfalls. All three come from the way Lipman et al.’s conditional paths pair p_{\mathrm{init}} with p_{\mathrm{data}}, from a Gaussian and independently. Rectified flow, the subject of post #5, addresses each.

6.5.1 Curved trajectories

The conditional trajectories of the optimal-transport path are straight, but the trajectories of the marginal velocity field u_t are, in general, not. By Eq. 15, u_t(x) averages the conditional velocity fields u_t(x \mid x_1) under the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x). Where segments toward different x_1 cross, it averages different directions. The trajectories of u_t cannot cross, because the ODE has a unique solution through each point (§3.1), so they bend instead.

For the optimal-transport path the average is u_t(x) = \big(\mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}[x_1] - x\big)/(1 - t).

For Gaussian data the curved trajectories have a closed form. The marginal velocity field is then a case of Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden’s formula for Gaussian mixtures (their Proposition C.1) [9], and Lai et al. use it to show that the trajectories are not straight [64].

Let p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2) on the line, with \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} > 0. For independent x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} and x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, the point x_t = t\, x_1 + (1 - t)\, x_0 has mean zero, the variance V(t) = t^2 \sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 + (1 - t)^2 and the covariance t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 with x_1. So x_1 - (t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t))\, x_t is uncorrelated with x_t, and independent of it, since the two are jointly Gaussian. Its mean is zero. Given x_1, the point x_t has the conditional path p_t(\cdot \mid x_1) (§6.1), so p_t(x_1 \mid x) is the distribution of x_1 given x_t = x. Writing x_1 as the difference above plus (t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t))\, x_t and conditioning on x_t = x, the posterior mean is \mathbb{E}_{p_t(x_1 \mid x)}[x_1] = t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 x / V(t). Substituting it into the average,

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 / V(t) - 1}{1 - t}\, x

Writing the numerator over V(t),

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - V(t)}{(1 - t)\, V(t)}\, x

Cancelling 1 - t, a factor of the numerator, since t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - V(t) = t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 (1 - t) - (1 - t)^2 = (1 - t)\big(t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - (1 - t)\big),

u_t(x) = \frac{t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - (1 - t)}{V(t)}\, x

Since the numerator is half of V'(t) = 2t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 - 2(1 - t),

u_t(x) = \frac{V'(t)}{2V(t)}\, x

The trajectory from x_0 satisfies \frac{d}{dt} X_t = \frac{V'(t)}{2V(t)}\, X_t with X_0 = x_0. So does \sqrt{V(t)}\, x_0, since V(0) = 1 and its derivative is \frac{V'(t)}{2\sqrt{V(t)}}\, x_0. Since V is positive and continuously differentiable on [0, 1], the field u_t(x) is continuous in t and Lipschitz in x uniformly in t, so by the uniqueness of the solution (§3.1) the trajectory is

X_t = \sqrt{t^2\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}^2 + (1 - t)^2}\; x_0

It ends at X_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} x_0, and the segment between its ends is (1 - t + t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}})\, x_0. Since (1 - t + t\sigma_{\mathrm{data}})^2 = V(t) + 2t(1 - t)\sigma_{\mathrm{data}}, which exceeds V(t) for t \in (0, 1), each trajectory with x_0 \ne 0 runs strictly closer to zero than that segment, so it is curved for each \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} > 0. For \sigma_{\mathrm{data}} = 1, where p_{\mathrm{init}} = p_{\mathrm{data}}, the segment is the constant x_0, but the trajectory passes through x_0 / \sqrt{2} at t = 1/2. The flow contracts toward zero and expands again, because each x_0 is paired with points x_1 of both signs, whose velocities partly cancel in the average.

With p_{\mathrm{init}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and p_{\mathrm{data}} an equal mixture of two narrow Gaussians at \pm 2, the posterior mean of x_1 has a closed form as well, by the same formula of Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden. So the segments and the trajectories of u_t can both be drawn in one dimension, as Figure 11 shows below.

Segments from starting points near zero run to both modes and cross. The trajectories of u_t from the same region first move little, while the posterior p_t(x_1 \mid x) still puts comparable weight on both modes. They turn toward one mode once the posterior concentrates on it. An adaptive solver takes small steps where a trajectory turns, which is one reason why even the optimal-transport path needs 142 function evaluations on CIFAR-10 (Table 1).

6.5.2 A fixed coupling of noise and data

The bending is a property of the target u_t, not of the network, so a larger network or longer training does not remove it. The target is fixed by the coupling of p_{\mathrm{init}} with p_{\mathrm{data}} that the conditional path builds in. For each x_1 the conditional path starts from the whole of p_{\mathrm{init}}, so x_0 is sampled independently of x_1, and the pairs (x_0, x_1) have the joint density p_{\mathrm{init}}(x_0)\, p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_1). The objective of Eq. 27 samples its pairs in this way, and nothing in it changes the coupling.

A trained flow does pair each x_0 with one endpoint \phi^\theta_1(x_0), because its trajectories do not cross, so the pairs (x_0, \phi^\theta_1(x_0)) form a deterministic coupling. Flow matching has no step that trains on this coupling. Its trajectories are also not, in general, the straight lines of the motion of optimal transport from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}} (§6.3.1).

6.5.3 A Gaussian source

A Gaussian conditional path starts at m_0 = 0 and \sigma_0 = 1, so each conditional path starts at \mathcal{N}(0, I), and so does the marginal path, its average over x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. The initial distribution p_{\mathrm{init}} must therefore be this Gaussian. Each diffusion path of §6.2 starts at a Gaussian that depends on x_1, close to \mathcal{N}(0, I) for the VP path and to a wider Gaussian for the VE path.

Flow matching with these paths generates from Gaussian noise, but it cannot carry one data distribution to another, as translating images of one domain into another requires. The general conditioning of §5.2.2.1 allows other initial distributions, but Lipman et al.’s Gaussian paths, which condition on x_1 alone, do not use it.

7 Why This Matters

The velocity field that carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}} can be learned directly, by regression, without learning a score first. That was this post’s question. Flow matching fixes a probability path from p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}}, built from conditional paths whose velocity fields are known in closed form. Conditional flow matching regresses the network onto those fields, with the same gradient as the intractable regression onto the marginal velocity field u_t (§5.2.2). The continuity equation guarantees that u_t carries p_{\mathrm{init}} to p_{\mathrm{data}} (§4.5). Training never solves the ODE; only sampling does.

The answer joined two lines of work, on flows and on diffusion. Normalizing flows gave exact likelihoods but needed invertible layers with determinants that are inexpensive to compute (Part 2). Flow models removed that constraint, but maximum-likelihood training solved the ODE at each step, on a path that the likelihood left unspecified (Part 3). The probability-flow ODE of diffusion then showed that a flow can be trained by regression, on a path fixed by the forward SDE (Part 5). Flow matching kept the regression and made the path a choice.

Part 6 made that choice for Gaussian conditional paths, the diffusion paths among them. Those paths keep three pitfalls (§6.5). The trajectories of u_t bend where conditional trajectories toward different x_1 cross, each x_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{init}} is paired with x_1 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}} independently, and p_{\mathrm{init}} must be Gaussian.

7.1 What comes next

Post #5 addresses the three pitfalls above. It conditions on pairs of points from any two distributions, through rectified flow and stochastic interpolants, and develops optimal transport and Schrödinger bridges to choose the pairing. It then places diffusion inside flow matching as one path. Flow matching on the VP path learns the velocity field of post #3’s probability-flow ODE. Solving that ODE gives a diffusion model’s exact likelihood, and its solution transports Gaussian data optimally but not data in general. Score matching and flow matching become two parameterizations of one path.
